text: Siman 1
Personal practices. “Declare the signs” (Isaiah 41:23):

Before any study and before any mitzvah (commandment), and especially when giving charity, it is good to have thoughts of repentance, and afterward let Israel say: “For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, in fear and love and in love and fear, to unite the Name י״ה with ו״ה in complete unity, in the name of all Israel. May the pleasantness of Hashem our God be upon us,” and so on (Psalms 90:17). Pay no attention to anyone who makes light of this, as I wrote in the booklet Simchat HaRegel, with Heaven's help.

He should have in mind that he is fulfilling the commandment of Hashem, may He be blessed, to do His will, and that there are many secrets in the Torah and in the mitzvot; and his intention should be to repair the roots of the Torah and of the mitzvah.

He should set fixed times for Torah by day and by night, a fixed rule that is not to be broken. And at any time that he is free, even if he has already completed his fixed portion, the book of the Torah should not depart from his mouth.

How good it is to learn after prayer while still wrapped in the tallit (prayer shawl) and crowned with tefillin (phylacteries). Let him take to heart that in former times the wholehearted in Israel, and many others as well, wore tefillin all day long; and in this orphaned generation, let him at least learn some one portion in tefillin, even one he has learned before.

When he learns in tallit and tefillin, he should intend to unify the Unique Name in this way: let him arouse the fear of Hashem from the letter י, the love of Hashem from the first ה, the Torah from the letter ו, and the mitzvah (of tefillin) from the last ה; and let him unify the Unique Name in complete unity.

He should strive to let things pass and not insist on his due, for this is the whole of man. Let him take to heart that he has sinned much, and that how many times, by the thousands, he has acted against the will of Hashem, may He be blessed; he must repair it all, and it will be demanded of him. And how much can he manage of self-mortification, or what strength does he have to accept suffering? This counsel, from the mouth that speaks great things, our master Rabbi Moses Cordovero, of blessed memory, is a precious cornerstone: to let things pass and not insist on his due. Through this his transgressions are atoned, and it is better for him than self-mortification and fasts. There is much to say about this, but I must be brief; it is a pearl beyond price, a remedy for everything, and long-lasting. This is hinted in the verse “I have exalted one chosen (בחור) from among the people (מעם)” (Psalms 89:20): בחור has the numerical value of גבורה, severity, for he removes the judgments; and מע״ם is the initials of מעביר על מדותיו, “he who lets things pass.”

Seek peace and pursue it (Psalms 34:15). This is the trait of Aaron the priest, who loved peace and pursued peace (Avot 1:12), and it is the elixir of life. If they said this about seeking peace with others, how much more so must he seek peace with the members of his household and his relatives. Know that wherever there is strife, the Divine Presence departs, Heaven forbid, for she is the mother of peace; and a house in which there is strife is a dwelling place of the Other Side, Heaven forbid.
Above all, let him be at peace with his wife, and take care to honor her, and in every detail let him have in mind the honor of the Divine Presence; these are ancient matters.

But with sweet words he should guide her in the service of Hashem, in modesty and proper conduct, and keep her far from evil speech and the rest of the “order of women” and the “order of damages.” It is his duty to correct her and guide her, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said.

He should beware of anger, small or great, for it exchanges his holy soul for a soul of the Other Side; he himself becomes like idolatry, tearing his own soul, and all that he labored for all his days, behold, when his soul departs, it has passed and gone. Thus spoke the holy man, our master the Arizal (Rabbi Isaac Luria), of blessed memory: one given to anger has no repair until he works very hard not to become angry at all, and then he can begin to repair (Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh).

He should warn his wife very strongly not to become angry, for they said in the holy Zohar (the foundational book of Kabbalah): whoever joins himself to an angry person is as if he had joined himself to actual idolatry (Zohar II:182b). If so, even if the man is holy, when his wife is given to anger, what has the righteous man accomplished?

He should take care to give charity every day, at least a perutah (a small coin), and intend to unify the holy Name הוי״ה. Let him intend that his arm alludes to ו, his five fingers to ה, the coin to י, and the five fingers of the poor man or the charity collector to ה: “והי״ה, and the work of charity shall be peace” (Isaiah 32:17).

He should be very careful with charity, for in our time it rises up in place of a sacrifice; it atones even for deliberate sins and saves from death, and through it a person is blessed with many blessings, as is explained in Scripture and in the words of our Sages, of blessed memory.

Above all, he should take care that his charity be given in secret, and not tell of his charitable deeds, and certainly not praise himself for his charity and kindness. Even if it is not said outright, if he contrives ways with the intention of being praised, he is punished for it, for the service of Hashem must be without any ulterior motive. And if he intends it for the sake of Hashem but adds to it the wish to increase his own praise, it is a grave sin. A person who cares for his soul will think deeply about this and strive until his whole intention is for the sake of Heaven, and nothing more.

Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that his main charity should go to those who toil in Torah, strengthening the stumbling knees, as the verse says, “Send your bread upon the face of the waters” (Ecclesiastes 11:1), and “water” means nothing but Torah, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Kohelet Rabbah 11:1). If he is wise he will be quick to do this, for he fulfills several mitzvot at once: charity; supporting those who learn Torah; spreading Torah, since the Torah scholar will learn with a settled mind; and honoring the Torah and those who learn it. Giving charity to an ignorant person cannot compare with giving charity to one who is worthy, and his reward will be very great.

He should take care to hide his good deeds and his learning. If people praise him, let him remember that he has not done one ten-thousandth of his obligation, and let him not become proud, Heaven forbid, even in the slightest. His heart knows that if he did some good thing, how much more has he sinned and neglected his service and his Torah study; and even in his good deeds, how many foreign thoughts rose in his heart, and how much he fell short in those very deeds in intention, in unification, and the like.

He should read books of moral instruction regularly. Fortunate is he who sets a fixed study in the holy book Reshit Chochmah; from it he will recognize the lowliness of his deeds and the force of his obligation, and day by day he should reflect on his ways.

He should take care to do kindness with his body, with his words and his advice, and with his money, and to rescue the oppressed, but without becoming involved in any strife at all, for then his gain would be lost in his loss.
Siman 2
The order of the night: “Though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light to me” (Micah 7:8), my Rock and my Redeemer:

He should go to pray Arvit, the evening prayer, with the congregation. Before Arvit he should say: “Hashem of hosts is with us,” and so on (Psalms 46:8); “Hashem of hosts, fortunate is the man,” and so on (Psalms 84:13); “Hashem, save! May the King answer us on the day we call” (Psalms 20:10).

He should say: “For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence: I am about to pray the Arvit prayer, which Jacob our father, peace be upon him, instituted, to repair its root in the place on high. May the pleasantness,” and so on (Psalms 90:17).

He should take great care to pray properly, pronouncing the words correctly and as they should be, and think that he is blessing the King of glory; let him put on trembling and wrap himself in awe. Moreover, the attribute of judgment is the aspect of night, and it prevails now, so he must be very, very careful.

He should say the Shema (the declaration “Hear, O Israel”) with great intention, especially the passage “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4), for the deepest secrets of His unity, may He be blessed, are very profound. In saying the word אחד, “One,” he should be careful to say the א briefly, not lingering on it at all, and to prolong the ח and the ד; and he should intend that he accepts upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven with fear, with love and with great joy. And he should intend to give himself up for the sanctification of Hashem's Name, truly, with a whole and joyful heart.

He should say “Blessed be the Name,” and so on, in a whisper, as our Sages, of blessed memory, instituted (Pesachim 56a), and not like those who are not particular to say it in a whisper. Before “And you shall love” (Deuteronomy 6:5), he should accept upon himself the yoke of His commandments, may He be blessed, and especially the Ten Commandments, and above all “I am” and “You shall have no other,” which are hinted in the passage “Hear, O Israel.” “You shall not take in vain” is hinted in the word “And you shall love”; “You shall not covet” in the word “your house”; “You shall not steal” in the word “your grain”; “You shall not murder” in the word “and you will perish”; “Honor your father and mother” in “so that your days may be many”; “You shall not commit adultery” in the words “and you shall not stray”; “Remember the Shabbat (Sabbath) day” in the word “and you shall remember”; “You shall not bear false witness” in the words “I am Hashem.” He should have in mind that the passage “And you shall love” has forty-two words, the number of the Forty-Two-Letter Name; the passage “And it shall be, if you listen” (Deuteronomy 11:13), up to “And you shall place,” has seventy-two words; from “these words of Mine” to the end of the passage, fifty words, corresponding to the fifty gates of understanding; the passage “And He said” (Numbers 15:37), seventy-two words. When the prayer leader repeats “Hashem your God,” this completes two hundred and forty-eight, and he should intend that the two hundred and forty-eight limbs of his body and of his soul, in its three levels, be repaired.

He should intend to pray the Amidah (the standing prayer of eighteen blessings) with submission, and if he is able to say all the weekday prayers with tears, fortunate is he. Let his whole body tremble: for who is he to pray before the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose Name is praised by countless myriads of ministering angels, and many ministering angels are given permission only once in seven years, and so on (Chullin 91b); and he, a gnat full of sins, is given permission! Should he not tear open the closed chamber of his heart, at least to humble himself and to know what he is saying? Let him take to heart that he is praying facing the Land of Israel, Jerusalem, the Holy Temple and the Holy of Holies.

At the first bow he should intend יא, the yod of הוי״ה and the alef of אד״ני; at the second bow, the second letters, הד; when he says “We give thanks to You,” the third letters, ונ; and finally, at the close of the blessing of thanksgiving, the fourth letters, הי, to unite יאהדונהי.

At the beginning of the Amidah he should regard himself as poor and needy, for he is poor and a wayfarer, and none is so poor and wretched, lonely and in darkness, as one who is alone, like one standing in a grave; and let him put on trembling. Although the middle blessings, in their plain sense, are for our needs, yet all of them are hints and secrets; glorious things are spoken of them, tenfold, in the levels of the supernal attributes. In general he should intend that all of it is to bring about a great unification among the attributes.
In “Hear our voice” he should confess briefly, and resolve to be pious, giving pleasure to his Creator. The text of the confession is below, in item 126.

Therefore, even on a day when no supplications are said, he should say in “Hear our voice,” as a request: “May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that You grant us to engage in Torah for its own sake, and in mitzvot and acts of kindness, and that all our deeds be for the sake of Heaven. Grant us to complete the repair of our soul, in its three levels, in this lifetime, and sustain us with a good livelihood, permissibly, with ease and abundance” (and he should intend the Name דיקרנוסא , which comes from the verse “and pour out for you a blessing until there is more than enough” (Malachi 3:10), and from the verse “Lift up upon us the light of Your face, Hashem” (Psalms 4:7)), “and from before You, our King, do not turn us away empty-handed; be gracious to us and answer us,” and so on. And he should resolve to be pious, as was said.
At “Be pleased” he should regard himself as a servant, until the end of the Amidah.
He should be very careful in the first three and last three blessings to intend what he utters with his mouth, and especially in the blessing of the Fathers he should concentrate very much.

When he finishes, he should be careful in saying “My God, guard my tongue from evil,” and understand what he is saying: “To those who curse me, let my soul be silent, and let my soul be like dust to all” (Berachot 17a). The word “all” includes great and small, poor and rich, wise and foolish; how then can he afterward be resentful and get angry? The author of the book Charedim wrote, on page 79: every penitent should say “Guard my tongue,” and so on, with tears and with great intention.
He should take three steps back with submission and bow, like one taking leave of the King.
He should listen very attentively to the words of Kaddish (the sanctification prayer) and answer Amen properly. In Kaddish he should intend that אמן has the numerical value of אידהנויה.

At “Amen, may His great Name,” he should intend that the remembrance of Amalek be erased, for then His Name and His throne will be complete. One must answer “Amen, may His great Name be blessed” with all his strength and intention, yet he should not raise his voice so much that people mock the sound of his shouting, for he may be punished for giving occasion for others to sin; moreover, it looks like arrogance or like a joke. One who fears Heaven fulfills every view: he prepares himself to say it with strength, and his voice is moderate.

After every prayer he should say “It is our duty to praise” standing, for עלינו has the numerical value of ומעומ״ד, “and standing.” He should say it word by word. He should not say “But we bow and prostrate ourselves”; rather he should pause after the words “cannot save,” and say “And we bow,” and so on. He should say “and the seat of His glory” and not change it. It is an awesome praise, full of supernal secrets. Joshua son of Nun first composed it, and later Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai instituted saying it after prayer, as our master Hai Gaon, of blessed memory, wrote in a handwritten responsum. Our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, revealed its secret: it is to draw down the encompassing lights.
Afterward, at every prayer, he should say “Therefore we hope to You,” and at “speedily in the splendor of Your might” he should intend the final letters, כה״ת, a holy Name.
It is a good custom to say after every prayer “Of David: Hashem is my light and my salvation” (Psalms 27:1), especially from Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon) of Elul until Hoshana Rabbah.

When he comes home, or in the days of winter, the winter nights when he goes about his business to check his account books, he should not remove the fear of Heaven from himself. It is good to say between tasks: “I have set Hashem before me always” (Psalms 16:8); “Fortunate is the man who does not forget You,” and so on (Musaf of Rosh Hashanah).

It is good for him to accustom himself not to eat much at night, for this is good for body and soul; not like those who eat for pleasure, meat for themselves, many drinking and becoming drunk, for there is the portion of the Other Side. Woe to them!
He should take care to fix his study at night in the Mishnah (the first written code of the Oral Torah) or in the Zohar; or both together are good.

משנה has the letters of נשמה, “soul.” The disciples of the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote that when one reads the Order of Seeds, he should intend to repair the damage he did through forbidden foods, blessings said in vain and the like. When he reads the Order of Festivals, he should intend to repair his sins of desecrating Shabbat and the festivals. When he reads the Order of Women, he should intend to repair the damage he did through forbidden relations, oaths and vows. When he reads the Order of Damages, he should intend to repair his sin against Hashem in having harmed his fellow, for the harm itself must be paid for. When he reads the Order of Holy Things, he should intend to repair his holy soul, which he brought out into profane use, his carelessness in slaughtering and in examining, sins that carry the penalty of being cut off, and prayers without intention. When he reads the Order of Purities, he should intend to repair the damage he did through a menstrually impure woman, through a seminal emission, and through washing of the hands.

Nothing compares to learning Mishnah aloud, calmly, in clear speech. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that Asher son of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, stands at the entrance of Gehinnom (purgatory) and saves everyone who learns Mishnah; and this is what the verse says: “From Asher, his bread shall be rich (שמנ״ה)” (Genesis 49:20), which has the letters of משנה.

In reading the Mishnah he should at least try to understand the meaning of the words, even if he does not truly understand the meaning of the subject; for if he does not understand even the words, some have written that it does not count as learning at all.

The study of the book of the Zohar is exalted above all study, even when one does not know what it is saying, and even if he makes mistakes in reading it; it is a great repair for the soul. For although the entire Torah is Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, it is nevertheless clothed in many stories, and a person who reads and understands the stories turns his mind to the plainest meaning. But the book of the Zohar is the secrets themselves, openly revealed; the reader knows that they are secrets and hidden things of the Torah, only that they are not understood because of the limits of the one who grasps and the depth of what is grasped.

The time of midnight, it seems most likely, is twelve hours after midday, as in the French way of counting the hours. If he is awake he should say Tikkun Chatzot, the midnight lament, as arranged by our master the Arizal, of blessed memory (Sha'ar HaKavanot, Sermons on Tikkun Chatzot), and at the end of the verses of lament he should say: “Woe is me for the exile of the Divine Presence. Woe is me for the destruction of the Holy Temple. Woe is me for the burning of the Torah. Woe is me for the killing of the righteous. Woe is me for the desecration of His great Name and His holy Torah. Woe is me, for the enemy has prevailed. Woe is me for the suffering of all the worlds. Woe is me for the suffering of the holy fathers and the holy mothers. Woe is me for the suffering of the prophets, the pious and the righteous in the Garden of Eden. Woe is me for the suffering of the Messiah. Our iniquities have turned these away, our transgressions have prolonged our end, and our sins have withheld the good from us. Woe to the children who have been exiled from their father's table (Berachot 3a) for so long, for many evil years. Every generation in whose days the Temple is not rebuilt is as if it had been destroyed in its days (Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma 1:1).” “For my palace,” “Awake, please,” “Upon your walls,” and so on (Isaiah 62:6).

He should say Tikkun Leah in this order: “A maskil of the sons of Korah” (Psalms 42:1); “Judge me” (Psalms 43:1); “May He answer you” (Psalms 20:2); “Of David, a psalm: The earth is Hashem's” (Psalms 24:1); “May God be gracious to us” (Psalms 67:2); “Halleluyah, I will thank Hashem” (Psalms 111:1); “Wander, wander” (Isaiah 24:20); “When Nathan the prophet came to him,” and so on (Psalms 51:2). This order is the main one.

If he goes to sleep before midnight, he should try to fall asleep amid words of Torah. He should say the whole Shema standing, and intend that he says it standing in order to focus his mind. He should intend to fulfill the mitzvah of reading the Shema, since what he read at Arvit with the congregation was not at its proper time and he did not fulfill his obligation; therefore he now reads it to fulfill his obligation. It is more correct to read it at its proper time, with intention. He should intend to give up his soul at the word “One,” and that this be a repair, to bring out into the light the sparks of holiness that were scattered through him. He should intend to complete the two hundred and forty-eight words with submission and awe, and say the order of the Shema of our master the Arizal, of blessed memory (Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Shema Before Retiring). After the confession he should say this text: “I hereby accept upon myself the four death penalties of the court, stoning, burning, slaying and strangling, to atone for my many transgressions. May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that it be accounted to me as if I had been stoned, burned, slain and strangled by the Great Court in Jerusalem, through the four letters of אדני; and may what I have damaged in the twelve letters of Your three precious Names, הויה אהיה אדני, be repaired. May the Name ע״ב shine in the World of Emanation, the Name ס״ג in the World of Creation, the Name מ״ה in the World of Formation, and the Name ב״ן in the World of Action; may all the Names be united in complete unity, and may all the worlds be repaired with a complete repair.”

When he fulfills the mitzvah of marital relations, he should be very careful that no candlelight be visible at all, for it is a blemish to his soul and a danger to the child, and he will be reincarnated because of it.

They said in the Zohar: “Fortunate are the righteous, whose desire is always toward the Holy One, blessed be He” (Zohar II:11b), that is, even in their union. By this the righteous man, whose fear of Hashem is upon his face, is tested. Fortunate is he who conducts himself in holiness and purity, sanctifying himself in what is permitted to him. This is essentially what our Creator, may His Name be blessed forever, commanded us: “You shall be holy” (Leviticus 19:2), as the Ramban, of blessed memory (Ramban on Leviticus 19:2), explained: after He commanded us about forbidden foods and forbidden relations, it is still possible for a person to be a scoundrel within the permission of the Torah, for he may sate himself, sate and sate again, with every food that comes up on the table of kings, of whatever is permitted to Israel, and with many wives by marriage contract and betrothal. Therefore God spoke once, “You shall be holy”: to sanctify oneself in what is permitted to him; and they said this of his wife. Let him overcome his inclination greatly, to strip away the lust of the material within him, and intend only to fulfill His commandments, may He be blessed, with modesty and shame, for the whole earth is full of His glory (Isaiah 6:3). And let him teach his wife to have pure thoughts, for the child depends very, very much on its mother, as the early authorities wrote: even if the man sanctifies himself properly, a woman who comes toward him otherwise frustrates his plan, and he does not know that it is his undoing.

If it is after sleep, the man and the woman, if they are worthy, should take care to wash their hands first, to remove the evil spirit; otherwise there is danger, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said, “it should be cut off” (Shabbat 108b), and so on.

Let him remember that he will have to give a full account even for idle conversation; the beams of his house and the wood of his bed, these are his witnesses (Chagigah 16a). He must be very, very diligent and gird himself with strength, for the evil inclination entices him with a double enticement, and all its thoughts are to make him sin; it removes the fear of Heaven through the vanities of this world, which perish and are lost, and all its arguments concern what appears good for the moment, as the verse says, “and it is a delight to the eyes” (Genesis 3:6). But one who comes to purify himself is helped (Yoma 38b).

If he takes care that it be on Shabbat and after midnight, fortunate is he, and fortunate are his children after him, for the Other Side will not rule over them; and he should intend to unite the Beloved and His beloved above.

When their hands are clean and they are properly covered, they should have in mind that it is for the sake of the mitzvah, and say “A psalm of David: Hashem is my shepherd” (Psalms 23:1). If it is after sleep, when he still has to say the blessing over the Torah, he should not say it aloud, only in thought.

He should take care to teach his wife, at the proper time, the signs that Jacob our father, peace be upon him, handed down to Rachel our mother (Megillah 13b), which my great-grandfather explained in the book Chesed LeAvraham (Chesed LeAvraham, Even Shetiya, Maayan 2, Nahar 61), may his memory be for the life of the World to Come.
Afterward he should wash his hands and pour clear water around his bed.
If he went to sleep before midnight, he should try to rise in the last watch of the night to say Tikkun Chatzot.
He should cover the vessel holding the water with which he washed his hands, for it is impure water, worse than urine.
Before the Tikkun he should say the morning blessings, from the blessing on washing the hands up to “and I will bless them” (Numbers 6:27).

He should take care not to say any verse before the blessing over the Torah. Although in some communities the custom has spread publicly to say several verses and only afterward to say the blessings, they do not do well.

He should be very careful, when he rises from his bed, not to walk four cubits without washing his hands. Travelers especially must be careful about this, and before they lie down they should prepare a vessel to wash with and a vessel to receive the water. One who looks closely will warn his wife and his servants strongly to be careful about this, and will warn them to wash the hands of the small children properly, so that they do not make impure everything they touch and the Other Side rest upon everything, Heaven forbid.

He should not have water poured on his hands by a maidservant, even a Jewish one, and even if she washed her own hands first, because she is menstrually impure as long as she has not immersed; he wishes to purify his hands, and so he should not wash from one who is impure. Even for washing the hands before a meal, some have written that one should not wash from a menstrually impure woman.
When he dresses, he should take the garment with his right hand, pass it to his left, and then put it on.
Siman 3
The order of the day: “By day Hashem commands His kindness” (Psalms 42:9); so He gives to His beloved (Psalms 127:2):

The first law of the holy book Shulchan Aruch, the Code of Jewish Law (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1), is: he should strengthen himself like a lion to rise in the morning for the service of his Creator. And if, Heaven forbid, his inclination rules over him in the very first law, so that he does not fulfill it, let him consider again what he will do in his end. Therefore a person should rouse his good inclination against his evil inclination (Berachot 5a), and take to heart also the first gloss, “I have set Hashem before me always” (Psalms 16:8), for the whole earth is full of His glory (Isaiah 6:3), and, as it were, He sees his laziness and his lingering in sleep at the time to rise for the Shema and for prayer. Let him be ashamed and abashed, and then he will leap like a deer to the service of Hashem. It is proper that he not speak of his affairs from the moment he rises, and that his first speech be to bless his Maker; all the more so since it is a fence, so that he is not drawn into talk with his household and his servants before he has blessed and prayed. He should relieve himself and wash his hands, for this is a very great need, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said that by this he accepts upon himself the complete yoke of the kingdom of Heaven (Berachot 14b–15a); and there is a secret in the matter. All this applies even if he could sit for several hours without needing to relieve himself; if he does need to, then it is obvious, as it is written, “One who needs to relieve himself should not pray” (Berachot 23a); and they wrote that these are the initials of “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel” (Amos 4:12).

He should be very quick to go to the synagogue, and run on his way to the synagogue, yet all with composure, so that he does not cause those who see him to stumble by mocking him and calling him a foolish pious man.

It is a great need and an obligation to put on tzitzit (the fringed garment) and tefillin at home, then go out, kiss the mezuzah (the scroll on the doorpost), and walk to the synagogue wrapped in tzitzit and crowned with tefillin. The holy Zohar (Zohar III:265a) is very strict about this.

At the least he should put on tzitzit and tefillin in the synagogue courtyard, before entering the synagogue door. As he enters he should pause a little and say: “And I, through Your abundant kindness,” and so on (Psalms 5:8); “In the house of God we walk with the throng” (Psalms 55:15); ברג״ש, “with the throng,” has the numerical value of אבגית״ץ.

In saying “Through Your abundant kindness” (Psalms 5:8), he should have in mind that he is not worthy to come into the house of Hashem and to visit His sanctuary (היכ״ל has the numerical value of אדני), but he relies on the merit of Abraham, hinted in the words “through Your abundant kindness”; on the merit of Isaac, hinted in the words “I will bow toward Your holy sanctuary,” for Isaac was sanctified on Mount Moriah; and on the merit of Jacob, hinted in the words “in awe of You,” after the verse “And he was afraid and said, How awesome,” and so on (Genesis 28:17). As he enters he should bow toward the Ark that holds the Torah scroll, for holiness rests there.

He should take care that the fringes are as they should be. Those who are meticulous check the fringes constantly, lest there be some defect and his blessing be in vain, and worse, that he be wearing a garment without fringes.

He should take care to put on two pairs of tefillin, one according to the order of Rashi and one according to the order of Rabbeinu Tam. Although they said that this shows arrogance, that was in their time; now many are accustomed to wear them, and in the Land of Israel nearly most of the scholars and the wise are particular about wearing both pairs, and many God-fearing householders also wear both. The custom spread on the basis of the writings of our master the Arizal, of blessed memory (Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Tefillin 9), that they are an obligation, and not because of doubt, as the halachic authorities wrote. As for what some wished to base on the words of the Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, it is a mistaken text, as we explained in a responsum at the beginning of the booklet Chaim Sha'al, with Heaven's help.
How very careful one must be not to take his mind off the tefillin at all. It is a difficult thing and the punishment is great; therefore great diligence is needed.
Before he begins the verses of praise, he should say a prayer that I have compiled and arranged; you will find it below, with Heaven's help (at the beginning of the booklet Tziporen Shamir).

He should make himself like a servant and begin the verses of praise, saying everything from the prayer book. Let him know before Whom he stands, and say all the words properly, with fear and trembling, in a low voice.
He should be very careful in saying the passage of the daily offering and the passage of the incense, and it is good to count the eleven spices on his fingers.

From the moment he begins the verses of praise he should take care not to speak at all, for all the verses of praise are to repair worlds; how then can he interrupt with idle talk? Indeed, according to the Kabbalah it is hardly proper even to study psalms and the like between the connected sections of the verses of praise, for all these verses, and this order, are set and arranged according to the secret and the supernal mysteries, and it is not proper to interrupt with other words of Torah that do not belong there by their measure. If this is so for words of Torah, woe to one who speaks idle words! The holy Zohar (Zohar II:131b) is very, very strict about this, for he brings disgrace upon the Divine Presence, Heaven forbid. According to the law as well, once he has begun “Blessed is He who spoke,” it is forbidden to interrupt, for the blessing “Blessed is He who spoke” was instituted in the days of the first Sages of the Mishnah, before the verses of praise, and the blessing “May it be praised” after them; how then can he interrupt in between?

He should intend to fulfill the mitzvah of reverence for the synagogue and the mitzvah of reverence for the Divine Presence that rests there. It is proper to take care not to speak in the synagogue at all, even when it is not the time of prayer, according to the plain meaning of the words of the holy Zohar (Zohar II:131b).

When he says “and You rule over all” (I Chronicles 29:12), he should give three perutot to charity. He should say the Song of the Sea with great joy, like one standing at the sea and being saved; if he does so, his sins will be forgiven, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said.
He should be careful in answering the Kaddish prayers and “Bless” with fear and love and great joy.

He should gird himself with strength for the Shema, in all that was written above. He should intend to fulfill the positive commandments of reading the Shema, of loving Hashem, of the unity of Hashem, of giving up his life for the sanctification of Hashem's Name, of remembering the Exodus from Egypt, and the mitzvah “and you shall see it” (Numbers 15:39). Whoever reads the Zohar Chadash (Zohar Chadash, Acharei Mot) will see with his own eyes how great, how mighty and how severe is the punishment of one who does not concentrate in the Shema, and, corresponding to it, the great good, hidden and wondrous, that awaits one who fulfills the mitzvah of the Shema properly.
He should join the blessing of redemption to the Amidah with very great alacrity, and intend that he is facing the Land of Israel, Jerusalem, the Holy Temple and the Holy of Holies.
He should clear away his phlegm and spittle and anything that disturbs him before he begins to pray; and know before Whom you are praying (Berachot 28b).

In the Amidah he should intend that all of it is to repair the supernal attributes. He should take care to pray in a whisper, the main thing being that he himself not hear his voice, yet that he pronounce the words with his lips properly; for this, care and composure are needed.

He should be very careful that his ears are attentive to the prayer leader's repetition of the Amidah, so that he answers Kedushah (the sanctification) and the Amens properly, and not an “orphaned Amen,” and so on.
In the first three blessings, the intention in answering Amen is “the thing is true”; in the middle and last ones, the intention of Amen is “so may it be.”
In answering Amen to blessings he should intend that אמן has the numerical value of יאהדונהי.

He should take care to be expert in the laws he needs when he prays, such as the law if he made a mistake in “Who makes the wind blow and the rain fall,” or in the request for rain, or in “May there rise and come,” and the like; for if not, he will not know what to do when a doubt arises. To begin with, he should take care to pray from the book, and be alert so that he does not forget and have to go back, and his blessings be in vain.

In saying the confession he should humble himself greatly and feel regret, and his mind should be set on repenting; for otherwise the Wrath (הקצ״ף) will respond and give the accuser an opening to say, “See this man, an insolent man (חצו״ף), who says the confession without thought and regret, as if speaking to a common person,” Heaven forbid. The soul of one who fears Hashem refuses to be comforted over the confession that people say in a single breath, as if speaking to their servant, Heaven forbid. Woe to us!
In reciting the Thirteen Attributes he should take care to say them properly, with full intention, for their secrets are many, and these things stand at the heights of the world.
In falling on his face he should take care not to rest his head on his hand, which is a danger, but on his arm, at the elbow or near it.

When he says “To You, Hashem, I lift up my soul” (Psalms 25:1), we have a tradition that in this orphaned generation one should not intend to give up his life for the sanctification of Hashem's Name, for it is dangerous to intend this while falling on the face; he should only intend that he gives himself over, in the mystery of death, for the keeping of the Torah and the mitzvot.

If it is a day of Torah reading, he should not speak while they take out the Torah scroll, for this is a time of mercy, and there is a great secret in it. He should rejoice at seeing the Torah scroll, honor it and kiss it. If he performs any of the mitzvot of the Torah scroll, he should rejoice in it. It is the custom of this city that one whose wife has entered the ninth month of her pregnancy takes care to perform, in that month, the mitzvah of opening the Ark; it is a fine custom, and it has support according to the Kabbalah. If he is called up to the Torah, he should intend to repair the damage he did to the honor of the Torah. If he rejoices at being called up, an abundance of holiness will flow onto him from the holiness of the Torah scroll.

When he goes up to the Torah, he should say the blessings over the Torah word by word, properly and aloud, so that the congregation will answer Amen. He should not be resentful about the place of the portion he is called to, that it is not what he thinks befits his honor, for all this is the scheming of the evil inclination to make him sin and to keep him from the service of Hashem. Rabbi Joseph Ezobi, in Ka'arat Kesef, spoke rightly to his only son, in his poem full of choice sayings.

Afterward he should finish his prayer properly, and intend to draw down abundance from world to world, for the whole order of prayer is a ladder set on the ground whose top reaches the heavens; it is all for a great need, mighty, vast and lofty, and angels of God ascend and descend on it (Genesis 28:12).

After prayer he should try to study the day's portion in the book Chok LeYisrael, for it is a fine arrangement, short and proper, and in a little time one merits to read the Tanach (the Hebrew Bible) and to learn Mishnah, Gemara (the Talmud) and Zohar. The God-fearing man has set it as a fixed rule that is not to be broken, for it is of enormous benefit to his soul; this faithful reading is a delight. He should also study the Tanach with the Targum (the Aramaic translation), as our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote; there he will find everything ready. However, there are many errors in it, and one must understand and notice the error. In the Prophets and the Writings he should study once the text and once the Targum. He should not concentrate on the meditations written there, for they are full of mistakes, nor should he say the prayers at the beginning of the book. (Now Chok LeYisrael has been printed in a fine and pleasant arrangement, with moral instruction and settled law for every day.)
When he comes home to taste something in the morning, he should take care with the blessing over the food and the drink, and that what he eats be the amount that requires an after-blessing.

If he eats pastry, there is a dispute among the halachic authorities as to how much he may eat and still say the blessing “For the sustenance,” and from how much he must say Birkat HaMazon (Grace after Meals). The most widely agreed view is that if he eats less than fifty-four drams, which are about five ounces of this city, he says “For the sustenance”; if he ate fifty-four drams or more, up to seventy-two drams, he is in doubt as to Birkat HaMazon, and he should not say Birkat HaMazon unless he eats seventy-two drams. Although some disagree, this view is the main one, and so several later authorities agreed.

He should say the blessing “For the sustenance” properly, for there are some who say the blessing and leave out parts from the start; they read one and skip three. All this comes from our sins and from the distractions of the vanities of this world, which in the view of the evil inclination are the main thing, while the service of Hashem, for which we were created, is secondary. Woe to us! See how carefully a man examines his coffee, whether it is good, and whether the cup it is in is clean and beautiful; but that the blessing is lacking and not as it should be, he does not care. And even in the blessing that he says, such as it is, he gestures with his fingers and laughs. Woe for that shame! He should not say an after-blessing over coffee, for many great later authorities hold that one does not, and so the custom has spread in the Land of Israel, in the regions of Turkey and in the land of Egypt, even though the author of Ganat Veradim, the master of that place, held that one should bless. And if in his city the custom has spread to bless, the God-fearing man should not bless, but should be discreet about it so as not to come to strife.

When he goes about his business, he should be very, very careful about many prohibitions, for there he stands ready either to fulfill the warning of Hashem, may He be blessed, or to transgress it, Heaven forbid. Among them are: robbery, theft, overcharging, falsehood, deceit, dishonesty in measure, in weight and in volume (Leviticus 19:35), deceiving people, the “dust of interest,” interest, “you shall not press,” withholding a hired worker's wages, a false oath, and going back on one's word; these, their offshoots and their like. Fortunate is he if he is saved from all of them. He should intend that he goes to do business to support his household with dignity and so that he not fall into want, and set his mind to be careful in everything the Torah warned about, whether by Torah law or by the words of the Sages, and all his deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.

He should trust in Hashem in his business and in everything: “And you shall remember that it is He who gives you strength to make wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18). He should not think that his success comes from the power of his mind and his sharpness, for everything is from Him, may He be blessed; how many sharp people are desperately poor, and how many fools are very rich!
He should take care to fulfill the positive commandment “On his day you shall give him his wage” (Deuteronomy 24:15), for it is an exceedingly great mitzvah, and the worker sets his heart upon it.
When he comes home at midday to eat a regular meal, he should bear in mind that the time of sitting at the table is a dangerous crossing.
If he does not drink wine at the table, he should drink less than a revi'it (a small measure) of water before washing his hands, for by this he exempts the water he drinks during the meal.

He should wash his hands with plenty of water, to fulfill the positive commandment of the Sages properly. He should take care to say the blessing “Who brings forth bread” properly, separating the words, and not bless as the gluttons and the guzzlers do, as Rabbi Menachem di Lonzano, of blessed memory, wrote in Derech Chaim.

He should intend that he eats in order to be healthy for the service of Hashem, may He be blessed. He should be careful to say all the blessings over enjoyment properly, and intend to draw spirituality and holiness into the food.

“The righteous man eats to satisfy his soul” (Proverbs 13:25). He should not be fussy about his food, and should be content with whatever is brought to him. Moreover, even by plain good sense it is a disgrace to be fussy about food and to bargain over the arrangement of the meal; hush, it is not to be mentioned (Amos 6:10).

In all weekday meals, whatever is beyond what he needs for his health goes to the Other Side. Therefore, if he is a person who cares for his soul, even if he is rich, he should limit his pleasures on weekdays, for pleasures on weekdays are like building a dwelling for the Other Side. Woe to him, for his limbs become impure, the Other Side rests upon them, and he has prepared weapons for the evil inclination to fight him until he goes down alive into the pit.

All the more so for those who make optional feasts on weekdays, and drinking parties: “there thrones were set” (Psalms 122:5), and it was called “drinking.” Do they not know that the Other Side takes its share at the head of the guests, and finds a place to make them sin and to cling to them?

Even on Shabbat and festivals, when it is permitted to eat and be sated, he should not eat with lowly people who engage in laughter and frivolity at the table, for then the table is turned into a serpent, the letters of the one being like the letters of the other, and Satan dances among them; may the Merciful One save us.

Were I to say, “I will recount” (Psalms 73:15) the whole order of damages that come one after another from optional feasts: I have already set this out at full length in the second treatise, and this time I have come only with headings, and let them be a reminder.

Laughter and frivolity are forbidden in every place and at every time, for they remove the fear of Heaven from a person. A sign for this is “Keep far from a false matter” (Exodus 23:7): שקר, “false,” is the initials of שחוק קלות ראש, laughter and frivolity. Even with his wife: they said that even for the light conversation between a man and his wife, he will have to give an account (Chagigah 5b), as it says, “He tells a man what his conversation was” (Amos 4:13). All the more so if she is menstrually impure, for they wrote that he should keep away even from looking at her face, and likewise from speaking with her; and your sign is “I was mute in silence, I held my peace” (Psalms 39:3), whose initials are נדה. And although in our times this caution is far from practice, since she is greatly pained by it and one must give her ease, nevertheless laughter and frivolity with her are forbidden by law, and our Rabbis made many separations.

He should take care not to touch his wife while she is menstrually impure, even her clothes, or to throw her anything, as long as she has not immersed. They said in the holy Zohar that there is no impurity as severe as the impurity of a menstruant (Zohar II:3a). How foolish are some men who are not careful about touching her hand to hand or her clothes! They bring harm upon themselves, cleave to the Other Side, laugh and act frivolously. It is a constant sin, and these matters are very grave: both because of the great impurity that cleaves to him, and also because it lets the Other Side take hold of them, and when she becomes pure it does not part from them; and so they go from evil to evil and leave their remnant to their children. Moreover, this shows that he does not believe in our Sages, of blessed memory, who forbade all this.

He should separate from her for the period of a day or a night close to her expected time; and if at times her period came earlier, he must afterward separate earlier and keep away because of the doubt. All this is required by law.
If a food is sweet to his palate and pleasing to him, and while he is still enjoying it he withdraws his hand in order to deny himself, it is counted for him as a sacrifice and an altar of atonement.

At every meal he should say some portion of words of Torah, and say “If I forget you, O Jerusalem,” and so on (Psalms 137:5), and think that the table of the Omnipresent in the Holy Temple was destroyed because of his sins, while what is set on his own table is full of rich food; and let him be pained by this.

He should take care to wash his hands with the after-meal water, lowering his fingertips, and take care that the water be little, for it is the portion of the Other Side; if he gives it more, it is given more to cling to him.
If there are three, even on a weekday, he should say Birkat HaMazon over a cup, and the one who leads should take care to drink a revi'it so that he can say the blessing “For the vine.”

He should wrap himself in the fear of Heaven like a cloak, and let trembling seize all his bones when he comes to bless the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were. He should intend to fulfill the positive commandment “And you shall eat and be satisfied, and bless” (Deuteronomy 8:10), and say Birkat HaMazon word by word, with fear and love and joy, as is proper.
He should take care to set times for Torah during the day in any case.

He should take care to read through all twenty-four books of the Tanach, over and over again. The early generations called the twenty-four books “Mikdash Yah,” “the Sanctuary of God,” and in the cities of the West they still call it “Makshiyah.” I asked them what is “kashya,” difficult, for them in it, and no one could explain; and I told them that they mean to say “Mikdash Yah,” and in the mouths of the common people it remained “Makshiyah.”

The special power of the book of Psalms is already known, and it is very awesome. He should take care to read a portion of it every day, or at least every week, so that Mishnah, Zohar, Psalms and the twenty-four books never leave him, and he returns to them again and again, as far as his strength allows. Your sign is “Their merit will protect” (זכות״ם יגן), the initials of Zohar, the twenty-four books, Psalms and the Mishnah; for studying them will protect him in this world and in the World to Come, without doubt.
The practices that the Rosh (Rabbeinu Asher) commanded his sons (Orchot Chaim of the Rosh) should be as frontlets between his eyes, and he should read them once a week.
Seder HaMitzvot Katzar, which the great Rabbi Shabtai HaKohen arranged, is a short order, fine and fitting. He should not fail to read and review it, and fortunate is he who reads it every week.

After eating, when he goes about his business, he should again prepare himself as he did in the morning, bearing in mind the many prohibitions before him: if he keeps them, fortunate is he, and if he transgresses them, woe to him, as was written above, in item 97. Now especially he must be careful, for he is sated and happy, and also, as the shadows of evening lengthen, the attribute of judgment begins to grow strong, and the evil inclination grows strong.

If he takes a walk, as he is accustomed, he should intend it for the sake of Heaven: that he walks in order to be healthy for the service of Hashem, may He be blessed, and so that his heart be at ease to conduct all his affairs properly.

If he is in the company of people, let him think that his feet have been brought into the bronze fetters of the evil inclination and that he has almost fallen into its hand, for how many kinds of forbidden speech there are among those who talk: evil speech, mockery, falsehood, flattery, belittling people, boasting and praising themselves for their knowledge, their conduct and their sharpness, matters bordering on obscene speech, false oaths, mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain, belittling scholars, questioning the decrees of our Sages, of blessed memory, and the like. If he has eyes of understanding, he will keep away from them, or at least be like a mute who does not open his mouth; for although hearing these things is also forbidden, at least he holds on to half. And when he is on his guard, he will be alert to their words and try to keep far away from them.

He should take care to say the Minchah (afternoon) prayer at its time and with the congregation, wrapped in the tallit and also crowned with tefillin of the order of Rabbeinu Tam, without saying a blessing on them, unlike the Matzat Shimurim, whom the Ramaz (Rabbi Moses Zacuto), may his memory be for the life of the World to Come, has already refuted. He should say: “For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, and so on: I am about to fulfill the mitzvah of the Minchah prayer, which Isaac our father, peace be upon him, instituted, to repair its root in the place on high. May the pleasantness,” and so on (Psalms 90:17).

In “Hear our voice,” in all the weekday prayers, he should confess, and say thus: “We acknowledge before You, with shame of face, in disgrace and humiliation, that we have sinned, done iniquity and transgressed before You; we have violated commandments of the Torah and of the Sages, and done what is evil in Your eyes. Behold, we regret with complete regret, and we return in repentance. May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that You grant us to return in complete repentance; forgive, pardon and atone for all our sins, our iniquities and our transgressions; fill all the Names that we have damaged, and bring out into the light all the sparks of holiness that were scattered through us, and may everything return to its original strength. Grant us to fulfill all Your commandments and to engage in Torah for its own sake; save us from the evil inclination, and sustain us with a good livelihood, permissibly, with ease and abundance, for Your service” (he should intend the holy Name appointed over livelihood, דיקרנוסא, which has the numerical value of חת״ך together with its three letters), “and from before You, our King, do not turn us away empty-handed.” He should intend the Names in thought only, and not utter them with his mouth.

If he wishes to take a fast upon himself, before he takes his steps back he should say: “Master of the worlds, behold, I am before You, conditionally, in a voluntary fast for tomorrow, from dawn until after the evening prayer. If I cannot, or do not wish to, I may stop when I say ‘A psalm of David: Hashem is my shepherd’ (Psalms 23:1), and there will be no sin in me. But may it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that You give me strength and health, and that I merit to fast tomorrow; accept me with love and favor, grant me to return in complete repentance, answer my entreaty and hear my prayer, for You hear the prayer of every mouth. Blessed is He who hears prayer.”

In the prayer leader's repetition he should take care to answer Amen to the blessings and Amen to the Kaddish prayers. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: a person should always be careful with the Minchah prayer (Berachot 6b); the care applies to all its details and matters, in general and in particular, for it is a time of judgment. There is a further reason according to the Kabbalah; and the first prayer in the world was the Minchah prayer of Adam, the first man.
Siman 4
Keeping Shabbat is the joy of our heart. May God be gracious to us and bless us (Psalms 67:2):
On Friday morning he should take care to read the weekly Torah portion, twice in the original and once in the Targum (Berachot 8a); and if possible he should read it in tallit and tefillin.

He should read each verse twice in the original and once in the Targum, and not like those who are accustomed to learn each short paragraph whole twice in the original and then read it in the Targum; and certainly he should not learn the whole weekly portion twice in the original and then read the whole of it in the Targum. One should not do so. The correct way is to learn each verse by itself twice in the original and then say it in the Targum, and so every single verse until the end of the portion; and there is a sound reason for this according to the Kabbalah.

After he has read the last verse of the portion twice in the original and once in the Targum, he should go back and read it again in the original alone, and then read the haftarah (the reading from the Prophets).
If on Shabbat they will read the haftarah of Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh, or the haftarah “Tomorrow is the New Moon” (I Samuel 20:18), he should read the haftarah of the portion.

Afterward he should say “Hashem reigns, He is clothed in majesty” (Psalms 93:1), and the Mishnah “With what may we light” (Shabbat 2:1), and say: “Rabbi Huna son of Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rabbi Ammi: A person should always complete his portions together with the congregation, twice in the original and once in the Targum, even ‘Atarot and Dibon’; for whoever completes his portions together with the congregation, twice in the original and once in the Targum, his days and his years are lengthened” (Berachot 8a–b). And he should learn a short passage of the Zohar; thus he will have read the Tanach, Mishnah, Gemara and Zohar. (Now, in the new Chok LeYisrael, Mishnah and Gemara from the Order of Purities, Zohar, moral instruction and settled law are arranged for Friday too, and it is a proper thing.)

He should make an effort to prepare some of the needs of Shabbat himself, to buy something with his own hand and the like, and intend to fulfill the positive commandment “And it shall be on the sixth day that they shall prepare what they bring” (Exodus 16:5). The disciples of the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote that whoever takes trouble himself, with joy, over the needs of Shabbat, his sins are forgiven.

He should try to have his hair cut before midday, and intend that he has his hair cut in honor of Shabbat and fulfills the mitzvah “You shall not round the corners of your head, and you shall not destroy the corners of your beard” (Leviticus 19:27). After midday, even on Friday, one should avoid it. Fortunate is he who lets his beard grow, as is the custom in Turkey, in the East and in the West. One who lives in the cities of Christendom, and is a merchant, and is compelled to trim his beard, should take great care to do it only with scissors or with a depilatory, and not with a razor, Heaven forbid; and may the good Hashem forgive.

Rabbi Judah the Pious, of blessed memory, commanded not to cut the hair on Rosh Chodesh, even when it falls on Friday, and I have seen many who are great in Torah who followed his command. He should cut the nails of his hands and feet; he may cut them in their order, and need not be particular about it the way Rabbi David Abudarham, of blessed memory, wrote (Abudarham, Laws of Blessings, Ninth Gate, Nail Cutting).

If possible he should immerse every Friday. It is good to immerse once to remove the filth and the impurity of a seminal emission and the like; and four more immersions, accepting the four death penalties of the court, to repair the damage he did in the four letters of the Names הויה אהיה אדני, and the damage he did in the worlds of Emanation, Creation, Formation and Action. Through accepting the four death penalties and the four immersions, the Names ע״ב ס״ג מ״ה ב״ן will shine in the worlds of Emanation, Creation, Formation and Action, and the holy Names and the worlds will be united. He should immerse once more to unite everything. Further, he should immerse to repair the damage he did through anger, by the power of אלף הה יוד הה, whose numerical value is that of מקוה, the immersion pool. Further, he should immerse to strip off the weekday garments. And two more immersions to receive the light and the holiness of Shabbat.
He should wash his face, his hands and his feet in hot water in honor of Shabbat, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 25b), and in this order; and there is a great secret in it.

He should make an effort to change his clothes: “Remove the garments,” the weekday garments, “and put on festive garments” (Zechariah 3:4), the Shabbat clothes. Fortunate is he who has special clothes for Shabbat from the sole of his foot to his head, so that no garment, small or large, that he wears on weekdays goes on him. In everything he does on Friday, whether for the needs of Shabbat, or washing, or dressing and the like, he should say aloud that he is doing it in honor of the holy Shabbat.

When the time of Minchah comes on Friday afternoon, it is a dangerous time for strife between husband and wife and among the servants, and the Other Side takes great pains then to stir up quarrels. The God-fearing man will subdue his inclination and not arouse any strife or resentment; on the contrary, he will seek peace and go in peace, and pray the Friday Minchah properly, with composure and with the repetition, for it is the time when the lights of holy Shabbat are revealed in the heavens above.
He should say the welcoming of Shabbat with joy. I have a tradition that “A psalm, a song for the Shabbat day” (Psalms 92:1) must be said standing.

When he kisses the hands of his father and mother after Arvit on Shabbat eve, he should intend to fulfill the mitzvah of honoring father and mother; and when he kisses his mother's hands, let him think that there is a secret in the matter.

He should concentrate greatly in Kiddush (the sanctification of the day over wine) and have thoughts of repentance, for saying “And they were finished” (Genesis 2:1) is to testify that Hashem created heaven and earth and rested on Shabbat, and a wicked person is disqualified from giving testimony; therefore he should have thoughts of repentance so as to be fit to testify. He should make Kiddush to fulfill the positive commandment “Remember the Shabbat day to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8), which our Sages, of blessed memory, explained: remember it with words said over wine (Pesachim 106a). All of it should be with fear and love and great joy. Since by Torah law he has already fulfilled his obligation in the prayer and the like, and also since “Keep” is the attribute of night, he should say this text: “For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, and so on. ‘Remember’ and ‘Keep’ were said in a single utterance (Shevuot 20b). I am fulfilling the mitzvah of Kiddush over wine, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained: ‘Remember the Shabbat day to keep it holy,’ remember it with words said over wine, to repair its root in the place on high. In Your great mercy, may it be accounted to us as if we had intended all that is fitting to intend. May this Kiddush rise before You together with the Kiddush of Your children who know and who intend properly, and may abundance and great blessing be drawn into all the worlds, and from there flow onto our soul in its three levels, so that we may serve You in truth and keep all Your holy Sabbaths all the days of our lives, in thought, speech and deed, with fear and love and joy. May the pleasantness,” and so on (Psalms 90:17).

After he answers Amen to the blessing of Kiddush, he should not interrupt with speech until he has tasted; and likewise after the blessing “Who brings forth bread” he should not interrupt until he has tasted. He should be very careful about this, for if he interrupted with speech before tasting after “Who brings forth,” and the speech was not about the meal, as “Take, it is blessed” (Berachot 40a) is, he must say the blessing again.

He should make great efforts to keep the three meals of holy Shabbat always, all his days. Even if he is a little ill or has some pain, he should not let any meal pass without making it, for the meals of Shabbat are supernal matters in the heavens. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, on the day of his passing, praised himself only for having kept the three meals and never neglected them. Therefore he should be quick to keep them with joy, rejoicing with trembling, without laughter and frivolity, Heaven forbid, for that is a great blemish; his whole aim should be to fulfill His commandment, may He be blessed, and to do what he was commanded. In this way his body will grow from holiness and become a sacred vessel for His service.

Immediately after Arvit he should come home, make Kiddush and eat. He should not do as some people are accustomed, who sit there an hour or two with their friends and companions, speaking idle words and the like, and cast the holiness of Shabbat behind their backs. “Do not walk in the way with them; keep your foot from their path” (Proverbs 1:15). Take care to join holiness to holiness: the three times “And they were finished” is said, in the Amidah of Arvit, after the Amidah, and in Kiddush, are the ones that are joined; and he should not interrupt between the holiness of Arvit and the holiness of Kiddush and the meal with the words of a grumbler, which pain the additional soul. He should intend that the first meal corresponds to Isaac our father, peace be upon him, and saves from the birth pangs of the Messiah; the second meal corresponds to Abraham our father, peace be upon him, and saves from the judgment of Gehinnom; and the third meal corresponds to Jacob, and saves from the war of Gog and Magog (Shabbat 118a). Fortunate is he who does the mitzvot truly for their own sake, with a pure and whole heart.

The third meal should be specifically after Minchah. One who has set his heart on the word of Hashem, and whose whole desire is to fulfill the mitzvah, should try to do it properly, without hesitation, for this is the whole of man (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

On Shabbat eve one does not read by the light of a lamp (Shabbat 12a). If he sets someone to watch him, it is permitted, and his wife can also watch him. But there is reason to fear that the watcher will fall asleep and doze off; therefore it is good to read psalms, so as not to lie down without Torah, and with Psalms one may be lenient for one who is used to them.

He should be very careful on Shabbat about telling a non-Jew to do work, even work forbidden only by the Sages, where it is not for the sake of a mitzvah, for it is a grave sin; and even if he tells him before Shabbat.
He should be very careful not to speak about business on Shabbat, for he desecrates Shabbat; the holy Zohar (Zohar II:47b) is very strict about this.

Although some permit going over past accounts, some forbid it, and one who guards his soul will keep away. Even if it were permitted, from it he may come to matters that bear on the future; therefore let him close the door, and it will be good for him.

On the Shabbat day it is strictly forbidden to stir up strife or to become angry; it is a sin twice as grave as doing so on a weekday. Especially with his household there must be much peace, love and brotherhood, for the honor of the Divine Presence.

The living will take to heart that all week he is busy with his affairs; at least on holy Shabbat let him learn, and not spend the whole of Shabbat in strolling, eating, drinking and sleeping. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that Sabbaths and festivals were given only for learning Torah (Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat 15:3). And for one who does not waste time, there is a time for everything.

“The Children of Israel shall keep the Shabbat, to make the Shabbat for their generations” (Exodus 31:16): its initials allude to ביאה לאוהל, “coming into the tent,” and it is an obligation to unite the Beloved and His beloved, with full intention. This is “an everlasting covenant” (ברית עולם), whose initials are ע״ב, the numerical value of חסד, kindness, from the side of kindness. And the final letters of בני ישראל את are יל״ת, the initials of “Hashem is before me always” (Psalms 16:8).

In summer, when they pray late in the synagogue and prolong the hymns, the time for the Shema passes; therefore after the morning blessings he should say the whole Shema. He should say the psalms of holy Shabbat, “Rejoice in Hashem, O righteous,” and so on (Psalms 33:1), with joy; their secret is high and exalted. But he should not shout at the top of his voice, for that removes the fear of Heaven and the reverence for the synagogue. Who is it whose heart would dare to shout before a king, and how much more before the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and in the synagogue, the palace of the King?

He should take care not to err in the Shabbat prayers by beginning “You graciously grant,” which is not a good sign, and is an unnecessary blessing. Therefore it is good always to pray from the prayer book, and to give it all his attention; perhaps then he will pray properly.

He should take care to hear the Torah portion from the reader by listening only, like one who has no mouth, in the secret of the listening ear. If they call him to the Torah, he should read very quietly after the reader, so that his voice is not heard.
He should take care to answer “Bless” and Amen to the blessings of those called up to the Torah and to the blessings of the haftarah, as is proper.

In the text of Musaf (the additional prayer) he should say “You established the Shabbat,” and so on. In the repetition of Musaf, at the verse “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4), when saying “One,” he should give himself over for the sanctification of Hashem's Name.

When he comes home, if his custom is to taste only some grain food, he should make Kiddush and drink a whole revi'it at once, so as not to enter into a doubt about the blessing “For the vine,” and then eat the size of an olive of pastry. If he is accustomed to drink coffee, he should remember to cover its blessing with the blessing “Who creates the fruit of the vine” of Kiddush; since the coffee is incidental, he must have it in mind, or it must be in front of him; otherwise he will need to say “By whose word all things came to be,” and afterward include “For the sustenance” and “For the vine” together.

He should try to eat fruit at intervals on holy Shabbat so as to complete one hundred blessings. He should be very careful with the Minchah prayer, for it is a time of favor. When the Torah scroll is taken out he should say “Blessed is the Name,” “Blessed is Your crown,” and so on (Zohar, Vayakhel). Afterward he should concentrate greatly in saying “Your righteousness,” and afterward make the third meal properly, as was written above.
Siman 5
“You shall go forth in the dance” (Jeremiah 31:4): to draw the holiness of Shabbat onward and store it away within the weekdays:

On Saturday night he should pray Arvit with intention, for the Other Side grows strong. He should always say “May the pleasantness” (Psalms 90:17) on every Saturday night that is followed by a weekday, and concentrate greatly in saying the words, not with shouting, for on the contrary, that drives away the intention.

He should try to have a wax candle for the blessing “Who creates the lights of fire,” and say the blessings of Havdalah (the separation at the end of Shabbat) properly, and immediately say the verses “May God give you” (Genesis 27:28). He should intend the one hundred and twenty permutations of אליהו, and ten more times אליהו, which make one hundred and thirty.

The fourth meal, after Havdalah, is a lofty wonder, and it saves from the beating of the grave. One who cannot make it with bread should make it with grain foods, and intend to leave a blessing from the holiness of Shabbat in the weekday meals.
One should not say the confession on Saturday night until after midnight.

In reading the passages of “twice in the original and once in the Targum” arranged in Chok LeYisrael, he should intend to keep in the day a light from the additional higher soul of the Shabbat that has passed. Therefore on Sunday he should think holy and pure thoughts and cleave with his heart to the love and fear of Hashem. Here is a rebuke to some people in the cities of Christendom, who on Sunday are free from trade and make drinking parties or set themselves to laughter. Woe to us! Let this hint suffice, for one must weep, lament and mourn that one who is called by the name of Israel turns his back and gives strength to the Other Side through clothing, pleasure and strolling; and it is written, “Do not rejoice, O Israel, unto exultation,” and so on (Hosea 9:1). And on Sunday the Temple was destroyed; woe and alas! For all this He will bring him into judgment.

On Monday, in reading the verses of “twice in the original and once in the Targum” in Chok LeYisrael, he should intend to keep in the day the additional spirit from the Shabbat that has passed. Therefore he should learn much Torah, and the sign is “a speaking spirit” (Targum Onkelos, Genesis 2:7). He should be especially careful about evil speech, as it is written, “but perverseness in it is a breaking of the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4).
On Tuesday, in reading these verses, he should intend to keep in the day the additional life-soul from the Shabbat that has passed, and he should seek to do kindness.
On Wednesday he should intend to acquire the light of the additional life-soul from the coming Shabbat, through reading the verses in that book, and seek to visit the sick and to do kindness.
On Thursday he should intend to acquire the light of the additional spirit from the coming Shabbat, through reading the verses in that book, and learn much, and so on, as we wrote for Monday.
On Friday he should intend to acquire the additional higher soul from the coming Shabbat, and prepare to meet his God with proper thoughts (see Tziporen Shamir, end of siman 4).
On Shabbat eve he should be ready to receive the addition to his soul in all its three levels.
On the day of holy Shabbat he should prepare himself to receive the addition to his soul in its three levels, from a source higher than at night.
Siman 6
The burnt offering of each new month in its month (Numbers 28:14); the crown of his God is upon his head (Numbers 6:7):

One who can fast on the whole vigil before the new month does a great thing. The essence of the fast is to search and examine very thoroughly what he has sinned throughout the month and to return in repentance, for the fast is a preparation to subdue his body so that he will repent. If he only fasts, without taking to heart what he has sinned and without repenting, he has done almost nothing.

On the fast of the vigil it is proper to learn the order of the offerings, that is: the whole portion of Vayikra, the portion of Tzav up to “in the wilderness of Sinai” (Leviticus 7:38), the passage of the libations, and the passage of unintentional idolatry in the portion of Shelach. Afterward he should say: “May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that the speech of our lips in the teaching of the work of the offerings be considered, accepted and favored as if we had offered a burnt offering, peace offerings, a thanksgiving offering, meal offerings and libations. If we have become obligated to bring a sin offering, or a certain guilt offering, or a suspended guilt offering, or an offering that varies with one's means, may our reading be considered as if we had offered the offering or the offerings we are obligated to bring; and if not, may it be considered as if we had only read Your Torah. In Your great mercy, forgive, pardon and atone for all our sins, our iniquities and our transgressions. May upright advocates stand before You to plead for us; be pleased with us, and rebuild the Holy Temple speedily in our days, and there we will offer before You the offerings we owe, the daily offerings in their order and the additional offerings according to their law. So may it be Your will.”
It is proper that the fast be before the molad, the moment of the new moon; if the molad is at midday, he should fast the day before.
On the eve of Rosh Chodesh he should take care not to forget to say “May there rise and come.”
On the eve of Rosh Chodesh marital relations are permitted, and his intention should be to unite the Beloved and His beloved, and for the sake of Heaven.
Some are accustomed to light the lamp on the eve of Rosh Chodesh; and it is proper to make it different from the eve of Shabbat.
It is proper to add some dish in honor of Rosh Chodesh.

Before Musaf he should remove the tefillin. If after prayer he wishes to put on tefillin to learn his fixed study, he may put them on; and all the more so he should not refrain from putting on tefillin at Minchah because it is Rosh Chodesh.
He should not say the blessing over the moon until seven full days have passed from the molad.
He should gird himself with strength to say the blessing over the moon with intention, for he is greeting the Divine Presence (Sanhedrin 42a); and let him rejoice with trembling (Psalms 2:11).
He should take care that it is shining well; if there is even a thin cloud over it, he should not say the blessing.

It is proper to go out toward the moon to bless it. If he has some ailment, he may bless from the window. If he is troubled by the wind, because he is a little ill and fears that it may harm him, and perhaps the time will pass, he may bless when he sees it from the window through the glass that people call jam, provided that he sees it shining and bright.
He should not look at the moon except before he says the blessing, for the Ramah wrote that it is forbidden to gaze at it, according to the Kabbalah.

He should say the blessing over the moon word by word, calmly and in clear speech, for after all he is saying that he greets the Divine Presence; how then can he send forth his words in haste and casually, as if swallowing something holy (Numbers 4:20), as though the earth swallowed the words of the blessing (Exodus 15:12)?

He should say “Blessed is your Former, blessed is your Maker, blessed is your Owner, blessed is your Creator,” and not like those who are overly clever and say them in the order of the worlds of Emanation, Creation, Formation and Action, from below to above; for the version of our Sages, of blessed memory, in the Midrash (Masechet Soferim 20:2) spells יעק״ב. I also saw that the great kabbalist Rabbi Nathan Shapira, may his memory be for the life of the World to Come, protested against those who change it, and explained the version יעק״ב according to the Kabbalah, and one should not move from it. However, a long time afterward I saw that the Ramaz disagreed with Rabbi Nathan. When he says “May fear and dread fall upon them” (Exodus 15:16), he should intend the initials, which are a holy Name. There is a great special power in saying the blessing over the moon, to be saved from an enemy and from all evil, if he says it properly.

After “David, king of Israel, lives and endures” (Rosh Hashanah 25a), he should say Amen three times, and intend that אמן has the numerical value of יאהדונהי; Selah, forever. He should believe with complete faith that the Holy One, blessed be He, will redeem us, and we await His salvation.
