After the blessing over the moon he should not say “It is our duty to praise” and “Therefore we hope to You” up to “in the kingdom of the Almighty,” as has spread without knowledge in some towns; rather, after “It was taught in the school of Rabbi Ishmael” (Sanhedrin 42a), he should say “Peace be upon you”; and the wise will understand. Let this remark suffice, short and strong. This is a great principle: one should not follow any custom until he knows the root of the custom, from our Sages, of blessed memory, or from the authentic writings of the Arizal, of blessed memory, or knows a reason for the custom as good as a source.
Siman 7
A proper path for the months of the year:
The month of Nisan

It is proper to say the passage of the prince of each day on its day, and after it the prayer, except that he should not say “If I, Your servant,” and so on; rather he should say this text: “May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that our reading in the Torah of the order of the offering of the prince, so-and-so of the tribe of so-and-so named there, and so on, his offering that he brought for the dedication of Your holy altar, be considered and favored, and may it be accounted as if we had attained,” and so on.

He should make great efforts that the koshering of vessels by boiling be done according to the law and the halachah. People do many stringencies and cleanings that are not needed, and neglect things required by law, because they have not studied the books; therefore he must find someone expert to be present at the time of the koshering.

With the matzah, very great care and alacrity are needed: the workers must keep working the dough constantly; once the matzah has been rolled out, while it is still in the hand, they should at once perforate it and put it into the oven; and the baker should be expert, so that the matzah does not come out puffed up and the like.

The thoughtful man will give all his attention to whatever touches the law of chametz (leavened food), and especially to the matzah and the food he eats on Pesach (Passover), for this is the very essence of this holy festival. He should not let the clothing the household needs confuse his mind in place of the needs of his soul; enormous care is needed.
He should instruct the members of his household to clean and pick through everything well, especially the things bought for food, such as salt, coffee and the like.
Our Sages, of blessed memory, wrote that whoever guards himself from chametz on Pesach, even from the slightest amount, can be sure that he will have a good year.

He must give thought and look into the matters of this holy festival that concern the soul, and Heaven, seeing his good intention, will help him; we have a tradition that one who comes to purify himself is helped (Yoma 38b), and it is written, “He will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence” (Psalms 84:12). Therefore he must prepare himself and his heart to do all that is in his power.

He should try to say the blessing over the trees in the days of Nisan. The meticulous insist that it be specifically in Nisan and that there be two trees, and they go out to the field to say the blessing.

He should concentrate greatly in this blessing, for it is for the repair of the souls that are reincarnated in the trees of the field and in the grasses at this time; and he should ask for mercy on them.

On the night of the fourteenth, in the search for chametz, he should not stand in the house like an officer, walk through its length and breadth, and nothing more; rather he should truly search and examine every kind of place, perhaps he will find something that was forgotten or not seen. If he does not do so, it is almost a blessing in vain.

After “All leaven” he should say: “May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that You grant us to search out the plagues of the houses of the soul, in which we have acted foolishly by the counsel of the evil inclination, and grant us to return in complete repentance. And You, in Your mercy, help us and assist us for the sake of the glory of Your Name, and save us from the prohibition of chametz, even the slightest amount, this year and every year. So may it be Your will.”

In the day he should try to burn the chametz himself, for the mitzvah is greater when done by oneself (Kiddushin 41a), and also so that he will be quick to destroy it at once. He should nullify it and say: “May it be Your will, Hashem, our God and God of our fathers, that You have mercy on us and save us from the prohibition of chametz, even the slightest amount, us and all the members of our household and all Israel, this year and every year, all the days of our lives. Just as we have removed the chametz from our houses and burned it, so grant us to remove the evil inclination from within us always, all the days of our lives; and grant us to cleave to the good inclination, and to Your Torah, Your fear and Your love always, we, our offspring and the offspring of our offspring. So may it be Your will.”
It is good to say the text of “All leaven” three times, at night and in the day, for such is the way of the Sages; and pay no attention to one who wrote the opposite about a similar matter.

On the eve of Pesach he should take care to immerse in a ritually pure mikveh (immersion pool), for a person is obligated to purify himself for the festival (רג״ל) (Rosh Hashanah 16b). He should intend to receive holiness from the holy Names ע״ב and קס״א, whose numerical value is that of רג״ל. He should be quick in making the matzah of the mitzvah on the eve of Pesach, and be present there, and exert himself greatly in this. Kneading the dough and taking trouble over rolling it out is a great repair for his atonement. Before kneading he should nullify all the crumbs and all the bits of dough stuck on, as the dust of the earth. He should set his attention on purifying his heart, his thoughts and all his ways, for the essence of the purification of vessels is the vessels of the soul, the limbs of the body, in which is the leaven of the evil inclination.
It is the custom to sing Hallel (the psalms of praise) while rolling out the matzot on the eve of Pesach, in memory of the Hallel that was said while making the Pesach offering.
He should arrange the plate for the night himself, and this is the arrangement of the plate according to the Kabbalah.
Then he should go to the synagogue and concentrate greatly in Arvit, for very many are the supernal mysteries and the great lights in the heavens, the greatest of the great, heaps upon heaps.

Completing the Hallel in the synagogue: its secret is high and exalted. The authorities, of blessed memory, wrote that even if he is in a city where it is not said, he may say it with a blessing by himself, and several rabbis have done so in practice.

Let him see that this night shines like the sun with the strength of supernal lights; therefore the evil inclination makes itself a key and seeks a pretext to enter into one of the members of the household or the maidservant. The wise man has his eyes in his head (Ecclesiastes 2:14): calmly he will lock the door, and pass over everything, removing strife and bringing in love; and fortunate is he.

Warnings and matters concerning the order of “Kadesh, Urchatz,” the Seder (the Passover night ritual), we have already written, in our poverty, in the booklet Simchat HaRegel (Simchat HaRegel, Simanei HaSeder); go, please, and see, for there are some necessary things there. And the God-fearing man, while his soul still cleaves to Hashem, his soul will teach him to add more and more, for abundance comes forth from the source of his soul when Hashem favors his ways, to purify and sanctify him in everything that pertains to the repair of his soul, in the ways of alacrity in the mitzvot, in the joy of a mitzvah and in cleaving to Him, may He be blessed. These are things that have no fixed measure (Peah 1:1); if he merits, more is added to him.

After the Haggadah (the telling of the Exodus) he should say the whole Song of Songs in a joyful voice, in this time of joy, for “the time of singing has come” (Song of Songs 2:12), and all the upper worlds above shine and glow.
The custom has spread to drink coffee after the Seder, but without sugar. On the second night some are lenient with other drinks.

Smoking the pipe on a festival is permitted by law, but it is good to be strict on the first day of the festival; all the more so since a certain great man dreamed of an outstanding rabbi and adjured him by the Name of Hashem to tell him what is said in Heaven about smoking the pipe, and he answered him that one who smokes on a festival is cursed, one who smokes on Tishah B'Av (the fast of the Ninth of Av) is placed under a ban, and one who smokes in the bridal chamber is excommunicated. I saw this dream written by the great man who dreamed it, and there are other things in it, and it seems to me that it was written on it that the dream was in the year 424. But on the second day of the festival the great sages of the world were not strict.
Since one who does not smoke refrains only as a stringency, it seems that he may hand the pipe to one who smokes on the festival.

When the Torah scroll is taken out he should say the prayer printed in Tefillat Yesharim, “Master of the world, fulfill the requests of our heart,” which was composed by our master the Arizal, of blessed memory; Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, found it written in his prayer book in his pure and holy hand.

On a festival there is no third meal, for according to the secret there is no relation to a third meal, and no stringency applies to it. He should make Kiddush in the morning, drink a revi'it of wine, and eat an olive's size of grain food from matzah of a kind with which he does not make his meals throughout Pesach. For matzah, which is his bread on Pesach, even if it is enriched, cannot take the blessing for grain foods; its law is like bread, since it is his bread. Therefore he should try to have a difference in the matzah he eats in the morning, so that it is not of the kind of matzah of the meal, for example matzah made with eggs. But if it is made with eggs, they must be eggs alone, and it must be made more quickly than one made with water, and he should not mix wine into it, out of concern for the doubt of Rashi, of blessed memory.

He should make great efforts with the counting of the Omer (the forty-nine days from Pesach to Shavuot), for its secrets are high and exalted, and he should try to count at least close to half an hour into the night.

He should be quick to make himself reminders so that he does not forget even one night when he does not count with the congregation; for he may forget in the day as well and no longer be able to count with a blessing, and according to one view all the blessings of the past nights were in vain and he has neglected a positive commandment.
On the night of the seventh day of Pesach, according to the authentic writings of our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, there is a great obligation of marital union.
On the eighth day of Pesach he may be lenient in something that he observes only as a stringency.
On the day after the festival he should try to make a fine meal, for there is a secret in the matter, and according to the plain sense too it is a mitzvah.
Siman 8
Is it not truly good? It will bear new fruit every month until the year is complete:
The month of Iyar.

It is the custom not to cut the hair in the days of the Omer. According to our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, this is not because of mourning, as the halachic authorities wrote; rather there is a secret in the matter. According to the Arizal, of blessed memory, one must not cut the hair from the eve of Pesach until the eve of the festival of Shavuot (the Feast of Weeks), and according to his view, everything the later authorities permitted, to cut the hair on Rosh Chodesh, or for a bridegroom and the like, and on the thirty-third or thirty-fourth day of the Omer, is all forbidden. Also what some wrote, that on the forty-eighth day it is permitted, is not so, for our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, cut his hair only on the eve of the festival itself. When the forty-ninth day falls on Shabbat, I saw in the handwriting of the wondrous, pious kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Sharabi, may his memory be for the life of the World to Come, that he wrote, in these words: “If the forty-ninth day falls on Shabbat, my opinion is not to cut the hair on Friday; but they compelled me to cut it. And a bridegroom is not permitted to cut his hair before the forty-ninth day.” End of his words. And I, the younger, in my limited opinion, hold that he should cut his hair on Friday if the forty-ninth falls on Shabbat, so as not to enter the festival unkempt, and this is the main view. However, concerning cutting the hair in the days of the Omer there are several different customs according to the plain law; leave Israel be (Pesachim 66a).
On the day of the Second Pesach he should increase his joy somewhat, for the day is holy.

On Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer, he should increase his joy in honor of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, may his merit protect us, for it is the day of his hillula, the anniversary of his passing. It is known that his will is that people rejoice on this day, as is known from the story of Rabbi Abraham HaLevi, may his memory be for the life of the World to Come, and other stories that we have heard and know from the mouths of holy rabbis. Some are accustomed to hold a study session on the night of Lag BaOmer with ten men, to learn the praises of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that are scattered through the Zohar and the Idra Zuta (Zohar, Ha'azinu); it is a fine custom.
The month of Sivan
Warnings about the learning on the night of the festival of Shavuot and the like I have written, in my poverty, in the booklet Simchat HaRegel; see there.

He should rejoice greatly on this holy festival, and be stirred that in His great kindness He gave us His holy Torah. He should immerse on the eve of the festival, and at dawn, after the night's order of study, according to the Kabbalah.

It is proper to learn Psalms on the day of the festival of Shavuot, for King David, peace be upon him, passed to his rest on this day; and on the holy day, the day of his hillula, the saying of his psalms will rise in favor all the more.

The Azharot, the poems on the commandments that people customarily study, follow the view of the Gaon who wrote Halachot Gedolot (Halachot Gedolot, Introduction). It is known that the Rambam (Maimonides) disagrees with him about many mitzvot; therefore it is proper to read the mitzvot as written briefly according to the Rambam's view in the first part of the Yad HaChazakah (Mishneh Torah, Positive and Negative Mitzvot), or in Po'al Tzedek by the Shach.
The day after the festival is very holy, and one should rejoice on it, as was written about the day after Pesach.
The month of Tammuz

In the days “between the straits,” the three weeks of mourning, he should take great care to lessen laughter and to lessen pleasure, and say Tikkun Chatzot with weeping; this is said only to add to what he usually does. For all the worlds are pained by the destruction of the Temple, and everything depends on repentance; and because of our many sins, every generation in whose days it is not rebuilt is as if it had been destroyed in its days (Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma 1:1), and pain is added in the last generation. If he considers this, the closed chamber of his heart will be torn open.

It is good to say the order of Tikkun Rachel every weekday during the three weeks, after midnight. So they practiced in the Land of Israel, may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days, according to the writings of our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, and it is a custom of the devout.

When he gives charity in these days, he should add to his intention the uplifting of the Divine Presence, our strength, for because of our transgressions our mother was sent away these many years. Woe to us! Alas for us! Let him be greatly stirred to return in repentance, and remember that she refuses to be comforted; she says: “There is no cluster to eat, no first ripe fig that my soul desires” (Micah 7:1).
The month of Av

He should add still more grief and sighing, and with bitterness sigh a sigh that uproots and breaks, in the Nine Days, “and yet a tenth in it” (Isaiah 6:13). He should not eat meat or drink wine on weekdays, and should lessen his enjoyment as much as possible.
On Rosh Chodesh Av we are accustomed to eat meat in honor of Rosh Chodesh.

On Shabbat Eichah, even if it is the day of Tishah B'Av or the eighth of Av, he should wear Shabbat clothes in honor of Shabbat, and certainly he should not say any lament. If in his place they say them, he should refrain, for the holiness of Shabbat bars every kind of mourning, small and great. We, the children of Sepharad, are permitted marital relations as well, according to the ruling of our master Rabbi Joseph Karo, of blessed memory (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 554:19), even if Tishah B'Av falls on Shabbat. Also at the final meal before the fast, when it is on holy Shabbat, he should eat meat and drink wine in honor of Shabbat, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the Talmud (Ta'anit 29b). But at the final meal on a weekday, he should eat only one cooked dish and no more. It is forbidden to eat cooked eggs, even inside the dish, if it is not his custom all year to put eggs in this kind of dish; and if he wishes to eat both the eggs and the dish, it is forbidden. A salad of raw greens in addition to the dish is permitted by law, but one should be strict.
On the night of Tishah B'Av he should tear open the closed chamber of his heart in reading Eichah (Lamentations). But among the laments there are some that it is good not to say.
He should afflict himself greatly in his bed, and take some of the stones of the place and put them under his head.

Everything that our Sages, of blessed memory, forbade on Tishah B'Av applies until nightfall, and one should not be lenient in anything after midday; only women are allowed to tidy the house a little, and this is to fix in their hearts the belief in the redemption.

Also the passages of consolation written in the book, at Minchah: one should not refrain from saying them, so as to fix in the hearts of the people that Hashem will redeem us in His mercy and fulfill for us all the consolations of His prophets soon.

After Arvit, when it is night, he should wash his hands and face entirely, put on leather shoes, and say the blessing over the moon, for it is a fitting time to announce the redemption, to bless the supernal moon, and to say “David, king of Israel, lives and endures” (Rosh Hashanah 25a).
On the night of the tenth and the day of the tenth as well, he should grieve over the burning of the Sanctuary.

He should not say the blessing “Who has kept us alive” on the tenth day, for even on Shabbat during the three weeks our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, did not say it, and all the more so on the tenth day.

On the fifteenth of Av he should increase his joy a little, for there is an elevation of the Divine Presence, as is written in the Zohar, part two, page 135. He should take care to add to his Torah study at night, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit 31a).
The month of Elul

This sanctified month is a time of repentance for all. He should take care to examine his deeds well and honestly: every night, before he sleeps and before saying the confession, he should examine and search his ways and his deeds of that day, confess and repent; and he should do so from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement). For he ought to do this every night all his days, as the righteous do, who are called “masters of the reckoning” (Zohar III:178a); at the least he should do so in these forty awesome days.

Whoever has the strength to rise for Selichot (the prayers for forgiveness), fortunate is he. First he should say all the blessings, then Tikkun Chatzot, and then Selichot. The main thing is to say them properly, in the low voice of supplication, understanding what he utters with his mouth, his eyelids streaming with bitter waters over what he has sinned. Let him see himself as standing for judgment before the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who knows his thoughts and his deceits; then his uncircumcised heart will be humbled. One should not shout like one standing in the street, a fool who does not understand what he is saying, who shouts a shout with a voice of song. If they were wise they would understand that, Heaven forbid, they inherit a double Gehinnom: they force themselves to rise and lose their sleep to come to the synagogue, and here too they have done nothing but shout. Are they not called Selichot, “pleas for forgiveness,” and not “shouts”? These two words should suffice for one who has a heart.

He should not, for the sake of saying Selichot, pray the prayer not at its proper time and doze in his tefillin, for his gain would be lost in his loss. It is better for him to pray properly and not say Selichot.
This is the essence of service: to keep the essentials and to add to them; not to make light of the essential and keep the addition.
If he can fast some day or days in the month of Elul, fortunate is he, provided that it is with an examination of his deeds and with making a fence so that he does not return to his folly.
One whom God has graced with wealth should redeem his sins with charity, and increase in these days his charity and his study of the Zohar, the Tikkunim, the Mishnah and Psalms.
Siman 9
From Tishri to Adar: the blossom has opened:
The month of Tishri
On the eve of Rosh Hashanah (the New Year) he should fast and examine his deeds, and in any case immerse.
He should pray Arvit of Rosh Hashanah with weeping and with very great intention, worried and trusting.
He should come home happy and perform the customary order, eating gourd, beets, leeks, apple in honey, dates, pomegranate and a sheep's head.
In place of black-eyed peas he may take small beans.
He should not eat fish on Rosh Hashanah, as the Rashbatz wrote, and there is some support for this in the Zohar.
Some are accustomed not to eat anything sour on Rosh Hashanah, not even lemons.
Before he lies down he should say psalms until sleep overcomes him completely.
If his wife's immersion for the mitzvah falls on the night of Rosh Hashanah, it is permitted, and he must immerse in the morning before prayer.

He should try to rise in the last watch of the night, or at least at the light of morning. He should refrain from hearing the shofar blasts that are customarily blown in the morning before prayer, for according to the law and according to the Kabbalah there is no place for these blasts, and to sit and do nothing is preferable.
He may drink coffee without sugar before prayer, so that his mind will be settled.
In the prayer he should be very, very stirred to say it with a broken heart, with supplication and weeping.

He should take care to hear the shofar blasts to fulfill the positive commandment, and think that there are great secrets in them, and Hashem will accept his intention in general. Running and returning, while hearing the blasts he should reflect on his sins. If the one blowing pauses, he should confess much, in a whisper, between the sections.

He should exert himself in the lofty and awesome Musaf, with weeping and with full intention, and truly regard himself as nothing; for because of our many sins, in this orphaned generation we are gnats. If the Sages of the Talmud, peace be upon them, said “we are like donkeys” (Shabbat 112b), for us to be gnats is an elevation, not humility, for we have become very poor in Torah, in mitzvot and in fear of Heaven. Let him be stirred and beg of the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, with a broken heart; perhaps Hashem will be gracious.

When he comes home he should eat the festival meal, with the fear of Heaven upon him. At least in these days he should fulfill “I have set Hashem before me always” (Psalms 16:8), thinking, when he lies down and when he rises, when he eats and the like, that he stands before Hashem, as is indeed the truth, for the whole earth is full of His glory. The Rambam already wrote about this at length in his book the Moreh (Guide for the Perplexed III:52), and Rabbi Moses Isserles brought it briefly at the beginning of his glosses to the Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, and we alluded to it above. Fortunate is he who merits this trait always; he will be called holy.

He should strengthen himself like a lion not to sleep on the day of Rosh Hashanah, and engage in Torah; for not all times are alike for sleeping and taking pleasure, and now is the day of judgment, when the whole world passes before Him, may He be blessed, like sheep. Although they wrote that after midday it is permitted to sleep, that was not said for us, who are full of sins, while the filth of the Other Side has spread through everything. Therefore it is very good to strengthen oneself and engage in Torah; and even with all this, perhaps it will avail, given our low state in such an orphaned generation.

After Minchah, close to evening, he should say the order of Tashlich (the casting away of sins), and exert himself in his intention. I, in my poverty, have arranged a prayer to say at that time, asking for mercy and arousing compassion; it is in Tziporen Shamir (Tziporen Shamir, Siman 12).
On the second night of Rosh Hashanah too he should say “Who has kept us alive” in Kiddush, and a new fruit is not needed.
He should perform the order of the first night, eating those things for a good sign: apple in honey, a sheep's head, dates, and so on.
As he did on the first night and day, so he should do on the second: with arousal, study of Psalms, little sleep, and prayers with intention and weeping.
He should try to fast during the Ten Days of Repentance, and take great care to speak little, to examine his deeds, to repent, and to increase charity and peace.

On the eve of Yom Kippur, although he eats as the mitzvah requires, the fear of Heaven should hover over him. He should take care to know the meaning of the order of the Temple Service that he will say on Yom Kippur, so as to understand the words he utters. In any case he should immerse, with great submission.

On the eve of Yom Kippur he should exert himself in saying Kol Nidrei (the annulment of vows), and ask forgiveness for the damage he did to the sign of the covenant, and for vows and oaths. He should intend that the supernal vow be annulled, and read the passage of the Tikkunim that concerns this.

He should put on trembling in his prayers, with weeping and a broken heart. Even if it seems to him that he accomplished something in the Ten Days of Repentance, let him believe with complete faith that it is all as nothing compared with the enormity of his sins; moreover, it is mere imitation, like a monkey's, given his lack of knowledge of what he has damaged, his small grasp of divine wisdom, and the weakness of his strength in fear and in cleaving to Hashem. In all that he asks, his intention should be also for the members of his household and for everyone who is of the root of his soul and close to his root.

He should not say the confession two or three times, as the congregation says it; this warning we have heard from the holy writings of our master the Arizal, of blessed memory. I, in my poverty, have arranged a simple confession that includes most of the things a person treads underfoot. I begin to say it when they begin to confess, and while I say it the congregation says all the confessions. It was printed in Mishmeret HaTaharah, which I arranged, and in Sansan LeYair.

After Arvit he should say with the congregation the first four psalms of the book of Psalms, for their secret is very great, to be saved from a nocturnal emission. It is good not to say any verse or meditation for this purpose, lest, Heaven forbid, since he is blemished, his words bear no fruit, and on the contrary the evil be provoked against him, Heaven forbid. Therefore let him fulfill “I dwell among my people” (II Kings 4:13), and this is enough.
It is proper to say the whole book of Psalms after Arvit, and between one book and the next to say the hymns of the seven who made a covenant, exactly as they say on the night of Hoshana Rabbah.
Afterward, if he can, he should learn the Idra Zuta (Zohar, Ha'azinu).

When sleep overcomes him greatly, he should say the order of the Shema with intention. While still wrapped in the large tallit, he should lie down wrapped in it, and also in some of his clothes; and if he can, his feet should be uncovered while he sleeps, and it will be good for him.

He should rise like a lion and learn Psalms. If he is concerned that by the time the congregation says the Shema its time will have passed, he should say it alone, with full intention, before beginning the verses of praise.
He should say all the prayers and supplications with a truly broken heart and with proper intention.
He should exert himself in the order of the Temple Service to understand what he utters with his mouth, and humble himself greatly, for through our sins we lack everything.
He should try to weep at the Torah reading, in the portion of Acharei, and to grieve over the death of Nadab and Abihu; it is very good for him, as is written in the holy Zohar (Zohar III:57b).

In the prayers of Minchah and Ne'ilah (the closing prayer), although his strength is spent from the fast and from all the great grief he has felt over his shortcomings in the service of Hashem, may He be blessed, let him gird himself with strength, for the hour is pressing. Let him be stirred and exert himself, and pray to Hashem to help him for the sake of the glory of His Name and give him strength to stand at his watch; and He will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.

In the Arvit prayer of the night after Yom Kippur he should try to say it properly, and exert himself, for the crowd shouts and rushes; therefore he should pray from the book, so that they do not disturb him.

When he comes home he should say the blessing over the moon by himself, properly, for the congregation, behold, they are in a great hurry. It is more correct to bless the moon before Yom Kippur, for several reasons.

Then he should eat to his heart's content, with great joy and with trust in His mercy, may He be blessed, and before he sleeps he should learn a little. Let him not forget what his lips and his heart uttered together: to repent, and to be embittered over the past. Therefore let him go to sleep in a good way, amid words of Torah.

Right away on the night after Yom Kippur it is good to try to do something on the sukkah (the festival booth), to fulfill “So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir, and Jacob journeyed to Sukkot” (Genesis 33:16–17). The wise man has his eyes in his head, to prepare something on the eve of Yom Kippur so that he can begin building the sukkah on the night after Yom Kippur.

In the light of morning he should rise to pray, go early to the synagogue and pray properly. This is the whole fruit: to show in every matter of service, in Torah and prayer, humility and charity and the like, on the day after Yom Kippur, that he is consistent, continuing with what he did in the Ten Days of Repentance and yesterday on Yom Kippur, and that his intention is to keep it all the days of his life; and Hashem is his help and his shield.

After prayer he should seek out the four species, and not let himself be concerned about what he spent on the eve of Yom Kippur, so that he will have a beautiful and splendid lulav (palm branch) and etrog (citron). He should also turn his eye to the sukkah, to build it properly. Let him take to heart: to buy jewelry and clothes for his household he spends the money gladly; let him reason all the more so that he should spend money with great joy to have a splendid etrog and a fine sukkah. And what will he answer if he is stingy in a matter of a mitzvah, not giving to Hashem from what He has given him? Will he not be ashamed and abashed, and become the disgrace of the base?

On the eve of Sukkot (the Festival of Booths) he should immerse in a mikveh to receive abundance from the Names ע״ב and קס״א, whose numerical value is that of רג״ל; one is obligated to purify himself for the festival (Rosh Hashanah 16b).

On the night of the holy festival he should go to the sukkah and have a chair brought, with a splendid cloak upon it, in memory of the seven supernal holy guests, the Ushpizin, somewhat like what is done on the day of circumcision, a chair for Elijah the prophet, may he be remembered for good. It is written in the holy Zohar that if they do not prepare a chair for him, he does not come (Zohar I:93a). This was the way of those who tremble at the word of Hashem: to prepare a chair for the seven supernal holy guests. Every night he should say in clear speech in the sukkah: “Enter, exalted guests,” and so on (Siddur, Ushpizin). He should make Kiddush, and intend in the blessing “Who has kept us alive” to cover the mitzvah of the sukkah as well.

On the night of the festival he should intend to eat an olive's size in the sukkah as an obligation. Therefore, with the olive's size over which he says “Who brings forth bread,” he should intend at once to fulfill his obligation and the mitzvah of eating an olive's size in the sukkah on the first night, which we learn from the Festival of Matzot through the words “fifteenth, fifteenth” (Sukkah 27a).

In the morning he should bind together the lulav, the myrtle and the willow with lulav leaves that he prepared on the eve of the festival, for with these the law of tying does not apply. He should say the blessing in the sukkah and make the waving motions: south, north, east, up, down, west.

He should go to the synagogue rejoicing and glad in fulfilling His commandments, may He be blessed, and in Hallel make four more sets of waving, in the way he did in the sukkah: at the first “Give thanks” (Psalms 118:1), once; at “Please, Hashem, save now” (Psalms 118:25), twice; and at the last “Give thanks” (Psalms 118:29), once.
It is good to make the Hoshanot processions right away, as is the custom of the Land of Israel, may it be rebuilt and established, as the Magen Avraham wrote.
He should take care not to taste anything at all, and not to drink even water, outside the sukkah.

In the days of the festival he should not remove the fear of Heaven from himself, and Heaven forbid that he rejoice with a joy that is not the joy of a mitzvah. Let him remember all the effort he made in the Ten Days of Repentance, and moreover that the day of Hoshana Rabbah is before him, and his judgment is still in doubt.

Some warnings for the festival, for Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days), Hoshana Rabbah and Simchat Torah we have written, in our poverty, in the booklet Simchat HaRegel, with Heaven's help; and your eyes shall see.

For the circuits on the night of Simchat Torah I have arranged, in my poverty, a general prayer and a particular one for each circuit, with Heaven's help. The general prayer is printed in the book Divrei Shirah, and all of them in Tziporen Shamir (Tziporen Shamir 12).

After the festival, in the month of Cheshvan, he should exert himself in the fear of Heaven and in Torah study for its own sake, for it is the beginning of the year, and it will be a good sign for the whole year. Now, since it is close to the Ten Days of Repentance, he must show and demonstrate that all he did was not mere outward show, Heaven forbid. If he now begins to throw off the yoke and grow lax in the service of Hashem, it will not be favorable, Heaven forbid. Therefore, on the contrary, let him make a good sign for the whole year, running like a hero in the study of Torah and in the mitzvot, according to the good hand of Hashem upon him.
The month of Kislev

In the days of Chanukah (the Festival of Lights) he should be very careful to light at the proper time, and to light himself, not relying on a child or a servant, for the mitzvah is greater when done by oneself (Kiddushin 41a).
It is proper to light with olive oil, the choicest way to do the mitzvah, and to beautify the mitzvah with clean and fine lamps; and all for the sake of Heaven.
He should be very careful not to forget “For the miracles” in the prayer and in Birkat HaMazon.
On Friday evening he should light the Chanukah lamp before the Shabbat lamp. On Saturday night it is correct to light after Havdalah; but each place follows its own custom (Chullin 18b).

If his eyes have not grown dark, he will not spend these sanctified days in laughter and frivolity; for in days of miracles, when we are obliged to give thanks to His Name, may He be blessed, how can he, in place of thanksgiving, sin and incur guilt? For one who has a heart, this is enough.
The months of Tevet and Shevat

They are harsh months, Heaven forbid, as is written in the Zohar (Zohar Chadash, Eichah). It is good to set a time every day to plead with Hashem that He save him, all his household and all Israel from every kind of calamity, and so on. He must be careful in his ways, so as not to give judgment an opening to rule over him, Heaven forbid.
The month of Adar

“The Jews had light and joy” (Esther 8:16); but he should beware of laughter and frivolity. The wise man has his eyes in his head (Ecclesiastes 2:14), as they explained in the holy Zohar; and fortunate is he who considers his ways, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Moed Katan 5a).

Let the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, be before his eyes: that one should give more in gifts to the poor than in a lavish feast and portions to friends (Rambam, Laws of Megillah and Chanukah 2:17). And so it is right, for gifts to the poor are a pleasure for the holy soul, holy for the present and holy for the World to Come, since the Holy One, blessed be He, sows charity and makes it bear fruit, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said; and this is the joy of the soul. The feast and the portions are pleasures of the stricken body, and it is fitting to do more in matters of the enduring soul and not in matters of the perishing body. He should take care to fulfill the mitzvot of the day: reading the Megillah (the Scroll of Esther) carefully, and the righteous man will contemplate the wonders of the One who is perfect in knowledge, that there was but a step between the enemies of Israel, and so on: “Had it not been Hashem who was with us” (Psalms 124:1); gifts to the poor, to worthy and God-fearing ones, with full hands; and sending portions of food to his friend. Let him recline at the meal, glad and rejoicing in the joy of Hashem, and with all that is left over; and let him tell the members of his household the power of the miracle.

“The drinking was according to the law” (Esther 1:8): to become merry (Megillah 7b), not to become drunk. He should be alert not to lose Birkat HaMazon, a positive commandment of the Torah; and Arvit with ten men.

Let there be nothing like this: laughing with women, even on Purim (the festival of Esther), or strolling with them if they are not of his household and his relatives. One need not be strict about strolling with his relatives, provided it is not arm in arm, as is the custom. For the prohibition of gazing at women and of being close to them is very great by law, and not merely a matter of piety; and it is written, “Hand to hand, the evil man shall not go unpunished” (Proverbs 11:21). The interpreters of hints said: fourteen (י״ד) times fourteen is one hundred and ninety-six, the numerical value of לא ינקה, “shall not go unpunished”; and this is what the verse says: י״ד לי״ד equals לא ינקה. It is further possible to hint that the words יד ליד לא ינקה have the numerical value of two hundred and fifty-four; add to them the word ביד, “into the hand,” and the total is the numerical value of ר״ע, “evil,” for he has fallen into the hand of the Other Side, which is the added word ביד. This is what it says: “Hand to hand, the evil man shall not go unpunished”: he is evil, and evil will come upon him. Your sign: יד ליד לא ינקה, with the word בי״ד, has the numerical value of ר״ע.

In general it is a great prohibition to listen to the songs of women singers, for a woman's voice is indecency (Berachot 24a); even much conversation the authorities forbade by law, and there is an explicit Mishnah: “Do not converse much with a woman; they said this even of one's own wife. Whenever a man converses much with a woman, he causes evil to himself” (Avot 1:5), for the Other Side, which is called “evil,” cleaves to him, and in the end he inherits Gehinnom, which is called “evil,” as our Sages, of blessed memory, said; and he goes from evil to evil. Yet they read and teach this chapter in the synagogue, publicly before the people, and translate it into the vernacular, and there is not even one who understands in his heart what he is saying and singing in the chapter. What will they answer on the day of reckoning? Will they say, “We did not know that it is forbidden”? They will rebuke them to their faces: “Did you not hear the chapter sung for many years in public?” And if they say that they are pious, and women seem to them like white geese (Berachot 20a), He who knows hidden things will rebuke them, and they will be ashamed, for they had pleasure from the voice, the sight and the scent; and who knows how many have stumbled. May the good Hashem forgive.

One who fears the word of Hashem will give his attention to all the warnings of our Sages, of blessed memory, and will not transgress with contempt even a light one, for a light sin draws a grave one, and for everything he will have to give “judgment and account” (Avot 3:1). For he himself is the one who rules that this thing is forbidden, as in the story of Rabbi Judah the Pious, of blessed memory, and the rich man to whom they brought a book, and he read aloud “You shall not round,” and so on (Leviticus 19:27). This is “to give judgment”: you give the ruling that it is forbidden; and afterward “account”: how many times he did that forbidden thing. So the words “judgment and account” fit well, as we explained, in our poverty, in our Nimukim, with Heaven's help.
Siman 10
On the things a person treads underfoot; let him be alert and sanctified:

These are the things that a person treads underfoot. They are frequent, and through our many sins the habit of them becomes nature, so one must strengthen himself greatly to separate from them before the sun grows dark. One must ask for mercy concerning this secret: “the beams of our houses are cedars,” the secrets of the houses of the soul, in which there is something that weakens them. Examine them; do not be like one who forgets, as though it were forgotten from the start, by the counsel of his inclination.

The good and upright way is to separate from them not out of fear of punishment, but out of awe of His exaltedness and love of Him, may He be blessed. First in the reckoning of sins is evil speech, which is equal to idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed (Arakhin 15b), and it bears fruits. Evil speech is speaking in disparagement of one's fellow, even if one says the truth. Over this let the grieving grieve, and let them shed streams of bitter water, for it is a very grave sin and a frequent one, and he, his friends and his household have grown up in it. Woe to us! Alas for our souls!

Pride and resentment are a grave sin, like denying the fundamentals of faith and worshiping idols (Sotah 4b), and the dust of such a person will not be stirred, and so on (Sotah 5a). Within himself he lays his ambush, and all his aim is that people should esteem him; toward one who does the opposite he is filled with wrath. All this comes from his pride and his insolence, and he forgets what he is: the lowest of the lowest of lowly creatures, since he angers his Creator, Heaven forbid.
One sin draws another (Avot 4:2), and he will come to grave anger, which is like idolatry (Shabbat 105b), and tears his soul.
From this he will come to take revenge, bear a grudge and hate his brother of Israel, and he continually transgresses several positive and negative commandments.

If his resentment is against a Torah scholar, he will open his mouth without limit against the scholars of the generation, and if he wishes to show off, he will say: “Apart from their Torah, the scholars are lacking in moral discipline, in fear of Heaven and in proper conduct.” The early authorities already explained the intention of the verse “Horror has seized me because of the wicked who forsake Your Torah” (Psalms 119:53): they say “apart from their Torah,” and this is “who forsake Your Torah.” And he displays signs of purity, saying: “The scholars of earlier times were the delight of Israel; but those of our time, their traits and their ways are harsh, and all their desire is to extract money,” and more of the like. But they do not want to know that the Torah scholar has dependents hanging upon him, and the house is full of young children, and lacks bread, and so on.

From this he will come to be upset and brood at the time of prayer, and how many prayers and blessings fly off into the air! The father of them all is pride and resentment, which do not come forth to teach about themselves alone, but after them their companions are brought: sins and guilts, general and particular. Woe for that shame, for one who is destined to rot in the grave, and who will long for the worm to eat him so as to be saved from judgment, as it says, “But his flesh upon him will feel pain, and his soul within him will mourn” (Job 14:22).

Taking honor in the disgrace of one's fellow is common among the thoughtless, and shaming one's fellow in public is not lacking. All of these are branches and offshoots of pride; look closely and you will find it, for the idolatry of pride has four hundred chapters (Avodah Zarah 14b), and it was the mother of all prohibitions.

Four groups do not greet the Divine Presence: the group of liars, the group of flatterers, the group of scoffers and the group of those who speak evil speech (Sotah 42a). Woe to us, for almost everyone stumbles in all of them, or in some of them! The whole purpose of a person's coming into this world is that he merit, by the power of his Torah and his mitzvot, to gaze upon the Divine Presence; for one who eats what is not his own, and so on (Jerusalem Talmud, Orlah 1:3). How then can he make himself a charm against seeing the majesty of Hashem, Heaven forbid?

Sadness and melancholy are also evil in the eyes of its Master, for through them he neglects the order of the service of Hashem and serves his Creator with an angry face, with weakness and heaviness of body; his thoughts alarm him and his reasoning is confused.

Robbery, with its branches, its offshoots and its boughs, the deceptions of the inclination and the Rosh’s rulings of gall and wormwood, are more numerous than can be counted; scrolls could not contain them. As long as robbery is in his hand, his prayer is not heard, as it is written, “I will not pass by him any more” (Amos 7:8), as our Sages, of blessed memory, said. He must come back in another incarnation, and there is no difference between much and little, for God will bring everything into judgment.
Covetousness is the father of impurity. Our Sages, of blessed memory, already said that a certain wicked man came, through covetousness, to transgress all the Ten Commandments.

Blessings in vain and without intention; hasty and clipped prayer, swallowing half the letters and several words; and taking the mind off the tefillin: through our many sins these are common, if not all of them, then some.

Desecrating Shabbat: through our many sins, by having work done by a non-Jew, by weekday talk, by business dealings, and by carrying some light things from the city to the field, many have stumbled and fallen.

Behold, all these and more: through our many sins, the one who does them almost thinks that they are not sins at all, and all this because of how habitual they are. The God-fearing man will be wise to save himself from them little by little, keep his matters private, and pour out his soul to Hashem to save him; and one who comes to purify himself is helped (Shabbat 104a).

This is the counsel that is counseled: “the counsel (עצ״ת) of Hashem, it shall stand” (Proverbs 19:21). It is to hold fast to three things, humility (ענוה), charity (צדקה) and Torah (תורה), whose initials are עצ״ת; for these three are wondrous for being saved from many sins, and his sins will be forgiven. Provided that he takes to heart what he has sinned, in detail, and resolves to return to Hashem and not to sin again; and Hashem will be with him.

Further, he should make great efforts that whenever he does a mitzvah or learns Torah it be with great joy, more than over thousands of gold and silver, for having merited to learn Torah or to fulfill His commandment, may He be blessed; and surely this will draw additional holiness upon him. Our master the Arizal, of blessed memory, said that he merited all his lofty and wondrous wisdom only through the great joy, without end, with which he rejoiced in learning and in the mitzvot.

He should make great efforts to raise his children to Torah and to the service of Hashem, so that they will be full of the fear of Hashem, good traits and proper conduct; for this great wisdom is needed. A small book has already been composed on this, called Orech Yamim. One must reflect much on this matter and go down into the depths and inner chambers of his children's hearts. He should pray to Hashem about this with weeping, that He save his children from sin, and that all his offspring be holy offspring without blemish, and so on.

Let the observer observe how, because of shame, a person neglects many mitzvot. For example, if he is on the road, he neglects the mitzvah of tzitzit and tefillin because of the nations of the world, so that they will not mock him. He is also ashamed to do some things of the fear of Heaven, so that the scoffers will not mock him. And if he sees some person among the great and wealthy commit a sin or belittle the words of the Sages, Heaven forbid, he is ashamed to protest. There is another kind: one whose inclination misled him and he committed sins, and he has recognized his sins very well, but he is ashamed to repent lest they mock him, and his friends say to him: “Yesterday we sat together, we like you and you like us, doing all the abominations of Hashem; what spirit has come over you? This is nothing but arrogance, to fool people,” and the like. Because of the shame he remains in the dust of murky matter, and goes from evil to evil. Already the great explorer of the text, our master Rabbi Moses Alshich, of blessed memory, explained by this the words of the prophet Jeremiah, chapter 3: “And the shame has devoured the labor of our fathers,” and so on; see there words spoken by a holy mouth, sweeter than honey. The wonder about this bashful man is: how is he not ashamed before the Creator, may His Name be blessed forever, whose glory fills the whole earth and who sees his evil deeds? And how is he not ashamed of the proclamation made about him when he goes out to the marketplace, “This one is rebuked by his Master, forsaken by his Master,” as is written in the holy Zohar; and all the birds, and all that are in the air, hear the proclamation, curse him and keep away from him? Behold, a person is ashamed to go out before people's eyes in a torn garment, or in one that has a stain of some dirt or grease; even if they gave him all the treasures of the world, he would not appear before people with his clothes torn or wearing a soiled garment. How then is he not ashamed, when the garments that matter most, the garments of his soul, are torn to shreds, with defects beyond number, a filthy and stinking garment? When his soul departs, he will wear that garment before all the host of heaven, and become a horror, a mockery and a scorn. His eye will see bands of destroying angels shaming him and angering him, and they will say to him: “You are the man who was so particular about his clothes, that they be white and pressed, silk and embroidery, ordered and arranged, and you were ashamed at the lack of the slightest detail in the order of your dress; how are you now dressed in a robe of contempt and purple, the red of the judgment decreed upon you, a torn garment, despised and plundered, whose name is filth?” Moreover, he will be ashamed before people whom he did not esteem at all in his life; and if they come near or speak to him, they will terrify him in their wrath. They have merited the World to Come, while he is handed over to myriads of harmful spirits and destroying angels, for desolation and disgrace, terrified and filthy, ugly, wasted and stricken. Therefore the essence of shame and submission should be this: how could one lower than a gnat, despised and loathsome, transgress the command of the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He! Let all his bones be seized with trembling as he says the confession; let him be ashamed and abashed before the King, humble himself greatly, and make fence upon fence so as not to sin again. Let him return to Hashem, and He will have mercy on him, and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon (Isaiah 55:7). And let him not be ashamed before those who mock him, nor be dismayed before anyone; and this is what we have learned: “Be bold as a leopard,” and so on (Avot 5:20).

There is a man who has gained a name for dealing faithfully in business and keeping his word, for whom even a movement of his lips counts as a deed, and he too praises himself that he is trustworthy: what goes out of his mouth will stand and so it will be. How can this man behave so in matters of the body, which perish and are lost, while in matters of the soul there is no liar like him? In the merchandise of this world he keeps his word, but in the merchandise of the World to Come, which is Torah and mitzvot, he changes his wages ten times, and he transgresses the oath he swore at the assembly at Mount Sinai, and also what he swore in his mother's womb, to keep all the mitzvot. Every day he reads the Shema morning and evening, “and to serve Him with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 11:13), and this service is prayer (Taanit 2a); and at once he rises to pray, and his heart is not with him. He does not know whether it is a prayer; only his lips move, and he does not know what he is saying, whether prayer, or stories and the like. He says “Please make sweet,” and so on (Berachot 11b), “and place understanding in our heart, to understand and to grasp,” and so on, “and enlighten our eyes in Your Torah,” and so on (Siddur, blessings of the Shema, Shacharit), “and we will meditate on them day and night” (Siddur, blessings of the Shema, Arvit), and the like; and after a hasty prayer he does not give a thought to whether there is any Torah in the world. He says “And let my soul be like dust to all” (Berachot 17a), and there is none as touchy and proud as he; and many more like these. Truly, his glory shall not be that he keeps his word, when, after he speaks before Hashem about Torah and service, he at once breaks his word; and the breaches are more than what stands. Likewise there is a man who is compassionate and soft-hearted: if he sees a poor man on a rainy day facing the cold and shivering, his compassion is stirred for him; and if he sees the poor man living in a small, narrow and dark room, he is amazed at the life of pain and the foul dwelling. And it is a wonder how he has no compassion on his own soul, which will be placed in the Gehinnom of snow, handed over to cruel ones, the harmful spirits who bite and kill, while he is in Gehinnom, a place of darkness and the shadow of death. Likewise there is a man who is careful about people's honor, with every kind of courtesy and compliment, and one wonders at him: how is he so complete toward people, while he leaves his soul full of defects and losses? How is he not alarmed and does not say: “Behold, I take pains to show courtesy and compliments to people, and if once I miss a point of courtesy I am pained. How then am I so far from completeness before the Creator of the world, the supreme King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, in whose service I fall short all the time, in prayer, in Torah and in the mitzvot that He commanded me? Instead of giving Him pleasure, for which I was created, I have turned my back, and my fear of Him has become a commandment of men learned by rote; and I am not particular about Torah and prayer one hundredth as much as I am particular about courtesy!”

When an awakening comes to him about the affairs of his soul and the service of Hashem, he should take hold of it at once, right away, for the evil inclination cools its heat and seeks to distract him. Therefore, get ahead of the wicked one: if your heart stirs with something good, turn it into action. He should reflect on his traits, shame, compassion and the like, and measure them against his soul and the service of Hashem. Let him be ashamed before the King who sees and knows the secrets of his heart, and have mercy on his soul, and on his father and mother, so that they will not suffer pain in the World to Come because of him. We have a tradition that one who comes to purify himself is helped (Yoma 38b), and Hashem will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence (Psalms 84:12); He also instructs sinners in the way of life (Psalms 25:8).

Here I have set my words before you, and your charge has kept my spirit, in all that you asked; since you are precious in my eyes and honored, I hastened and did not delay in matters of Heaven that the Holy One, blessed be He, asks for. The land has given its produce, from the short work that was written: three hundred and thirty-one hints. “And he planted a tamarisk” (Genesis 21:33): the oaks of Moreh, pointing with a finger, a hint there; and their number is as the number of the names Jacob Chaim Joseph David, with four for the words, corresponding to fear, love, Torah and mitzvah, read as four. Is he not rightly named Jacob (Genesis 27:36): the noble and pleasant, my friend, the honored Rabbi Jacob Pereira de Leon, may his Rock keep him and give him life; Jacob has chosen for himself abundant kindness, and he put on righteousness like armor and a helmet. And his brother, good and kind, the wise and noble, my friend who delights in kindness, a fruitful vine: may Hashem repay their deeds in all their righteousness, as a support and a stronghold for me, and may wealth and honor be theirs sevenfold. The blessing of Hashem, which makes fruitful, comes ever increasing, abundant wealth; may their storehouses be filled with plenty. I, I am the one who writes, two letters hidden, a scribe's inkhorn pressed by fleeting moments, reaching and not reaching, like one whose color cannot be seen, and all the color is forgotten. I arrange prayer and pray; and as for me, my prayer is fixed. I rejoice in their love, the delight of my soul.
Finished and complete; praise to God, Creator of the world.
Elijah's Opening

When he enters the synagogue, let him first of all utter the Opening of Elijah the prophet, may he be remembered for good. It is in the holy Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkunei Zohar, Second Introduction, 17a), and the holy rabbis have a tradition that it helps for the acceptance of prayer:

Elijah opened and said: Master of the worlds, You are One, but not in number. You are the Highest of all the high, the Hidden of all the hidden; no thought can grasp You at all. You are the One who brought forth ten rectifications, and we call them the ten Sefirot, the divine emanations, to conduct through them hidden worlds that are not revealed and worlds that are revealed. Through them You are concealed from human beings, and You are the One who binds them and unites them. Since You are within them, whoever separates one of these ten from its fellow, it is counted for him as if he had separated You. These ten Sefirot proceed in their order: one long, one short, and one in between. You are the One who conducts them, and there is none who conducts You, neither above nor below nor from any side. You prepared garments for them, from which souls fly forth to human beings; and You prepared a number of bodies for them, which are called a body in relation to the garments that cover them. In this arrangement they are called: Kindness, the right arm; Might, the left arm; Beauty, the torso; Victory and Splendor, the two legs; Foundation, the end of the body, the sign of the holy covenant; Kingship, the mouth, which we call the Oral Torah. The brain is Wisdom, the thought within; Understanding is the heart, and through it the heart understands; and of these two it is written, “The hidden things belong to Hashem” (Deuteronomy 29:28). The supreme Crown is the crown of kingship, and of it is said, “He declares the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10); it is the head on which the tefillin are worn (another version: a head on which tefillin are not worn). Within, it is יו״ד ה״א וא״ו ה״א, which is the way of Emanation. It is the watering of the tree, with its arms and its branches, like water that waters a tree, and it grows through that watering.

Master of the worlds, You are the Cause of causes and the Reason of reasons, who waters the tree with that flow; and that flow is like the soul to the body, which is the life of the body. In You there is no likeness and no image of anything within or without. You created heaven and earth, and brought forth from them the sun and the moon, the stars and the constellations; and on the earth, trees and grasses, the Garden of Eden, plants, beasts, birds, fish and human beings, so that through them the higher realms might be known, and how the higher and the lower realms are conducted, and how the higher and the lower are to be known. But there is none who knows You at all, and apart from You there is no unity (another version: unification) in the higher and lower realms, and You are known as Lord over all. Each of the Sefirot has a known name, and by them the angels are called; but You have no known name, for You are the One who fills all the names, and You are the completeness of them all; and when You withdraw from them, all the names remain like a body without a soul. You are wise, but not with a known wisdom; You understand, but not with a known understanding. You have no known place; it is only to make Your strength and Your power known to human beings, and to show them how the world is conducted with judgment and with mercy, which are righteousness and justice, according to the deeds of human beings. Judgment is Might; justice is the central pillar; righteousness is the holy Kingship; the scales of righteousness are the two supports of truth; the hin of righteousness is the sign of the covenant. All this is to show how the world is conducted; but not that You have a known righteousness, which is judgment, nor a known justice, which is mercy, nor any of these attributes at all. Arise, Rabbi Shimon, and let words be renewed through you, for you have permission to reveal hidden secrets, permission that has not been given to any person until now.

Rabbi Shimon arose, opened and said: “Yours, Hashem, are the greatness and the might,” and so on (I Chronicles 29:11). Listen, you on high! You who sleep in Hebron, and the Faithful Shepherd, awaken from your sleep! “Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust” (Isaiah 26:19): these are the righteous, who are from the side of that of which it is said, “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2); they are not dead, and therefore it is said of them, “Awake and sing,” and so on. Faithful Shepherd, you and the Patriarchs, awake and sing, to awaken the Divine Presence, who sleeps in exile; for until now the righteous have all been sleeping, with sleep in their eyes. At once the Divine Presence gives three calls toward the Faithful Shepherd and says to him: Arise, Faithful Shepherd, for of you it is said, “The voice of my Beloved knocks” (Song of Songs 5:2) at my door with His four letters, and He says by them: “Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one” (Song of Songs 5:2); for “your iniquity is completed, daughter of Zion; He will no longer exile you” (Lamentations 4:22). “For my head is filled with dew” (Song of Songs 5:2): what is “filled with dew”? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: You think that from the day the Holy Temple was destroyed I entered My house and entered into settled land? It is not so; I have not entered, all the time that you are in exile. Here is a sign for you: “my head is filled with dew.” ה״א is the Divine Presence in exile; her completion and her life is טל, dew, and this is יו״ד ה״א וא״ו; and ה״א is the Divine Presence, which is not counted in ט״ל, but יו״ד ה״א וא״ו, whose letters add up to the number of ט״ל, which fills the Divine Presence from the flow of all the supernal sources. At once the Faithful Shepherd arises, and the Patriarchs with him. Thus far the secret of the Unification. (Fortunate is he who merits to say this every day: the words of the living God.)
